question: A  physician prescribes clonazepam to a patient with generalized anxiety disorder. Choose the false statement regarding its mechanism of action.

explanationHtml:
Remimazolam is the shortest-acting benzodiazepine. Its half-life is just around 37-53 mins, which is shorter than midazolam's half-life (1.5 - 2.5 hours).

Benzodiazepines can be classified as follows based on their elimination half-life:

  • Long-acting:
    • Flurazepam
    • Diazepam
    • Quazepam
    • Chlordiazepoxide
  • Intermediate-acting:
    • Alprazolam
    • Temazepam
    • Lorazepam
  • Short-acting:
    • Triazolam
    • Midazolam
  • Ultra-short acting:
    • Remimazolam

Note: Remimazolam was approved by the FDA in 2020.
question: Which is the shortest acting benzodiazepine?

explanationHtml:
Zonisamide does not belong to the Z-compound family.

Zonisamide is a sulfonamide anticonvulsant drug with no activity on GABA receptors. It inhibits the sustained, repetitive firing of spinal cord neurons by prolonging the inactivated state of voltage-gated Na+ channels. It also inhibits T-type Ca2+ currents. It is an adjunct drug for Parkinson's disease, partial-onset seizures, infantile spasm, mixed seizure types of Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, myoclonic, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures.

Z compounds are benzodiazepine receptor agonists. They are structurally related to benzodiazepines, but have less anticonvulsant and muscle relaxant properties. They are used for the treatment of insomnia. They include:

  • Zolpidem
  • Zaleplon
  • Zopiclone
  • Eszopiclone
question: A patient diagnosed with insomnia is taking a drug belonging to the Z-compounds family. Which of the following does not belong to this family?

explanationHtml:
Buspirone does not bind to the GABA receptor chloride channel complex.

Buspirone acts as a partial agonist at presynaptic 5-HT₁A autoreceptors, reducing the firing rate of dorsal raphe serotonergic neurons and thereby decreasing anxiety. It is used in the treatment of mild to moderate generalised anxiety disorder.

Other options:

Option A: Ethanol releases GABA and also has a binding site on the GABA receptor chloride channel complex.

Option B: Alphaxolone is a neurosteroid, and it acts through activation of GABAA receptors. These receptors are BZD-insensitive.

Option C: Zolpidem belongs to novel benzodiazepine receptor agonists called Z compounds. It binds to the BZD receptor present on the GABA receptor chloride channel complex.
question: A patient with generalised anxiety disorder is given a drug that does not bind to GABA receptors. Which drug was likely given?

explanationHtml:
The inverse agonist at the benzodiazepine receptor is beta-carboline.

Dimethoxy-ethyl-carbomethoxy-β-carboline (DMCM) impedes the action of GABA and can cause anxiogenic, convulsive, and memory-enhancing effects.

Other options:

Option A: Barbiturates (phenobarbitone) are agonists at an allosteric site on the GABAA receptor, facilitating the action of GABA receptors.

Option C: Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine receptor.

Option D: Picrotoxin blocks the GABA Cl- channel non-competitively.
question: Which of the following is an inverse agonist at the benzodiazepine receptor?

correctAnswer: B. It may be used to treat barbiturate poisoning
explanationHtml:
Flumazenil is the antidote used in benzodiazepine poisoning. It is not used to treat barbiturate poisoning.

Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine (BZD) receptor-specific antagonist (option A), competitively binding to the same site on the GABA-A receptor chloride channel where benzodiazepines bind (option D). It has no affinity for barbiturate binding sites on the GABA receptor Cl- channel complex. It competes with and antagonises BZD agonists, BZD inverse agonists, and Z-compounds.

It is available only for intravenous use(option C ). It is used to treat benzodiazepine overdose and for the reversal of sedative effects produced by benzodiazepines administered during general anesthesia.

options.text: It is a specific antagonist of benzodiazepine receptors
It may be used to treat barbiturate poisoning
It acts at the same site on GABA channel where benzodiazepines bind

question: A 33-year-old woman with suspected diazepam overdose was administered the antidote for benzodiazepine poisoning. Which of the following statements is false about this antidote?

explanationHtml:
Bicuculline is a competitive antagonist at the GABA binding site (α/β interface) on the GABA-A receptor. It blocks GABA’s action and prevents chloride influx, leading to neuronal excitation.

Other options:

Option A: Flumazenil is a competitive antagonist at the alpha/gamma interface of the benzodiazepine site of the GABA-A receptor. This is different from the binding site of GABA, which is the alpha/beta interface.

Option B: Picrotoxin blocks the GABA-A -Cl- channel non-competitively.

Option D: Propofol is an agonist at the GABA-A receptor.

Note: Muscimol is an agonist at the GABA-A receptor.

correctAnswer: B. 33-year-old man with history of acute intermittent porphyria
explanationHtml:
The administration of barbiturates is contraindicated in acute intermittent porphyria.

The rate-limiting enzyme in porphyria synthesis is δ-aminolaevulinic acid (ALA)-synthetase. Barbiturates are enzyme inducers - ALA synthetase activity is induced. Thus, barbiturates result in the increased synthesis of porphyrins and subsequent precipitation of acute intermittent porphyria.

Other options:

Options A and C: Barbiturates are used to treat anxiety and refractory status epilepticus.

Option D: Phenobarbitone can be used to treat kernicterus in newborns as it increases hepatic glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) enzyme activity and the conjugation of bilirubin.

question: In which of the following patients is the administration of barbiturates contraindicated?

explanationHtml:
The drug of choice for insomnia in blind people is tasimelteon.

Blind individuals develop a circadian rhythm disorder known as non-24h sleep-wake rhythm disorder. This is because the lack of light perception leads to loss of synchrony of their 24h circadian rhythm. Such people have nighttime insomnia and daytime sleepiness alternating with asymptomatic periods.

Tasimelteon is a selective agonist of melatonin receptors MT1 and MT2, and it helps entrain the circadian rhythm, restoring a more regular sleep–wake cycle in these patients.
question: A young woman, who is blind, presented with complaints of night-time insomnia. What is the drug of choice for her condition?

explanationHtml:
Suvorexant is an inhibitor of both orexin1 and orexin2 receptors. It is approved for the treatment of insomnia.

Orexins are produced in the lateral hypothalamus neurons and play a major role in maintaining the sleep cycle. Orexins promote wakefulness, while antagonists at orexin receptors enhance REM and non-REM sleep.

Other options:

Option B: Doxepin is a tricyclic antidepressant and has an H1 receptor antagonist effect. It is used for insomnia at lower doses.

Option C: Ritanserin is a 5HT2A/2C receptor antagonist indicated for insomnia.

Option D: Agomelatine is a melatonin receptor agonist and a 5HT2C receptor antagonist indicated for insomnia.
question: Your senior resident asks you to prescribe an orexin receptor inhibitor to a patient with insomnia. Which of the following drugs would you prescribe?

explanationHtml:
Diazepam and its long-acting metabolites can accumulate significantly in elderly patients with liver disease and, therefore, should not be used in such cases.

Diazepam is a long-acting benzodiazepine. It is metabolized in the liver by the cytochrome P450 enzymes to active metabolites like nordazepam. Nordazepam is further converted to oxazepam, which is then conjugated with glucuronic acid to form inactive metabolites.

In liver disease, the cytochrome P450 system is affected, and thus diazepam isn't metabolised. This may result in excessive sedation.

Lorazepam, oxazepam, and temazepam (Mnemonic: LOT) are eliminated by glucuronidation; therefore, they are safe in liver disease
question: A 68-year-old man with alcoholic liver disease is scheduled to undergo surgery. Which of the following benzodiazepines should be avoided in him?

explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario is suggestive of sleep-onset insomnia. Among the given drugs, the one prescribed for sleep-onset insomnia with the least effect on REM sleep is zolpidem.

Zolpidem is a non-benzodiazepine hypnotic. It acts as a selective agonist of benzodiazepine receptors and produces hypnotic-amnesic action. It shortens the sleep latency and prolongs sleep duration in insomniacs. It doesn't prolong total sleep time or alter NREM-REM sleep cycles. The effect on the sleep stages and REM sleep is less than that of benzodiazepines. Zolpidem doesn't show a rebound phenomenon on discontinuation, and it has low abuse potential. Other non-benzodiazepine hypnotics (Z-compounds) are zopiclone, eszopiclone, and zaleplon.

Other options:

Option A- Phenobarbitone can be used as a sedative and hypnotic, but it reduces REM and stage 3,4 sleep. It also disrupts the NREM-REM sleep cycle.

Options B and D- Both diazepam and alprazolam are benzodiazepines that can be used for sleep-onset difficulty. They are selective CNS depressants that produce sedation, relieve anxiety, facilitate sleep, suppress seizures, and reduce muscle tone. They also affect the REM sleep pattern - they decrease the time spent in REM sleep but increase the number of REM sleep cycles.

Note: Ramelteon is a hypnotic given for sleep-onset insomnia that acts as a melatonin receptor agonist. It hastens the sleep onset and increases the sleep duration.
question: A 38-year-old businessman came with a complaint of difficulty in falling asleep for a few weeks.  He recently closed his business due to large unexpected debt in the company. He says even though he is exhausted at night, it takes him hours to fall asleep. Which of the following drug can be prescribed to him which has the least effect on REM sleep?

explanationHtml:
Insomnia following frequent air travel describes a transient sleep disorder (including jet lag and shift work transition). The best and most effective pharmacological agent against this situation is ramelteon.

Ramelteon is a melatonin receptor agonist acting directly on MT1 and MT2 receptors.

  • MT1 receptor - Promotes the onset of sleep (hence used for induction of sleep)
  • MT2 receptor - Shifts the timing of the circadian system.

It reduces sleep latency and increases sleep duration, without next morning sedation or rebound phenomenon. It is considered to be more effective and safer than melatonin. Ramelteon is metabolized by the CYP450 enzyme system and should not be taken along with drugs or substances inhibiting CYP1A2 (ciprofloxacin, zileuton, and fluvoxamine) or CYP2C9 (fluconazole) enzymes. It should be cautiously used with rifampin, an enzyme inducer.

Its congener family includes:

  • Tasimelteon: Used for the treatment of chronic sleep disorders like non-24 h sleep-wake disorder. It is also used to treat insomnia in blind people.
  • Agomelatine: MT1 and MT2 agonist with 5HT2c antagonism used in major depressive disorder with insomnia.

[[figure-1]]

Other options:

Option A: Zolpidem belongs to a group of benzodiazepine receptor agonists called Z compounds. It binds to the BZD receptor present on the GABA receptor chloride channel complex. It is not a preferred drug for the treatment of jet lag due to excessive fatigue and impaired cognition on awakening.

Option B: Modafinil (wakefulness-promoting drug) is the drug of choice in narcolepsy, which is characterized by the tetrad of:

  • Excessive daytime sleepiness
  • Cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone)
  • Hypnagogic hallucinations
  • Sleep paralysis

Option D: Lorazepam is a benzodiazepine. It hastens sleep onset, increases total sleep time, and affects the REM-NREM cycle. It is also not a preferred drug for the treatment of jet lag due to excessive fatigue and impaired cognition on awakening.

question: A 45-year-old businessman presents to your OPD with complaints of insomnia. His job requires frequent travel to foreign countries and he always suffers from jet lag. Which of the following drugs would be the most appropriate for his treatment?

correctAnswer: A. Prolongation of Na+ channel inactivation
explanationHtml:
The most important mechanism of antiepileptic activity of phenytoin is the prolongation of Na+ ion channel inactivation.

Phenytoin is an anti-epileptic drug that preferentially binds to the Na+ channels in their inactivated state. It slows down the recovery rate of Na+ channels, thus limiting the propagation of the action potential. This prevents neurons from firing repeatedly and rapidly and is the most important mechanism noted at therapeutic concentrations of phenytoin.

Secondary mechanisms :

  • Enhances GABAergic inhibition → facilitates inhibitory neurotransmission.
  • Inhibits glutamatergic excitation → reduces excitatory synaptic activity.
  • Blocks voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels → decreases Ca²⁺ influx, which in turn reduces neurotransmitter release and alters K⁺ conductance during repolarization.
question: What is the most important mechanism of antiepileptic activity of phenytoin?

correctAnswer: B. Metabolism follows only zero order kinetics
explanationHtml:
The statement that phenytoin metabolism follows only zero-order kinetics is incorrect.

The pharmacokinetic characteristics of phenytoin are markedly influenced by its binding to serum proteins, by its nonlinear (dose-dependent) elimination kinetics, and by its metabolism by hepatic cytochromes P450 (CYPs).

Phenytoin follows first-order kinetics at lower concentrations, and as the concentration increases, the elimination changes to zero-order kinetics. The rate of elimination of phenytoin varies with the serum concentration.

Other options:

Option A: About 90% of phenytoin is bound to plasma proteins, mainly albumin. As a result, even minor fluctuations in the percentage of phenytoin that is bound can lead to substantial changes in the concentration of free (pharmacologically active) drug, which can impact both efficacy and toxicity.

Option D: Phenytoin is metabolised extensively by the CYP enzymes in the liver. It is primarily metabolized by CYP2C9/10 and to some extent by CYP2C19. Since its metabolism is saturable, co-administered drugs that compete for these enzymes can inhibit phenytoin metabolism, leading to elevated levels.

Conversely, phenytoin itself can induce the metabolism of other drugs that are substrates for these enzymes and lower their therapeutic effects (eg, Warfarin). Also, phenytoin is a potent enzyme inducer of CYP3A4- this increases the metabolism of other drugs like oral contraceptives.

Option C: As phenytoin blood levels increase, the liver’s metabolic enzymes (CYPs) gradually reach their maximal capacity. Once saturation is reached, phenytoin metabolism shifts from first-order to zero-order kinetics, and at this point, small increments in dose may result in a marked rise in plasma levels. This non-linear pharmacokinetic behavior makes therapeutic drug monitoring essential to keep levels within the narrow therapeutic window and prevent toxicity.

options.text: Metabolism follows only zero order kinetics
Metabolized extensively by the CYP enzymes in the liver

question: A known case of seizure disorder has been on long-term phenytoin therapy. Which of the following statements about this drug would be incorrect?

correctAnswer: D. ECG monitoring is not required when administering IV
explanationHtml:
ECG monitoring is not required when administering IV Fosphenytoin is an incorrect statement.

When fosphenytoin is administered too rapidly via IV during emergency management of status epilepticus, the most concerning toxic effects are cardiac arrhythmias, with or without hypotension and CNS depression. Therefore, continuous ECG monitoring is recommended during IV infusion due to the potential risk of arrhythmias, along with close observation of blood pressure and respiratory function, which should also be continued for at least 20 minutes afterwards. These complications can be reduced by using fosphenytoin at the rate of 150 mg of phenytoin sodium equivalents (PE) per minute.

Fosphenytoin is contraindicated in patients with heart conditions like sinus bradycardia, sinoatrial block, second- or third-degree atrioventricular block, and Stokes–Adams syndrome.

Other options:

Options A and B: Fosphenytoin is a water-soluble prodrug of phenytoin. Fosphenytoin is also extensively protein-bound, mainly to albumin. This binding is saturable, and fosphenytoin displaces phenytoin from protein-binding sites.

Option C: Hydrolysis of fosphenytoin yields phosphate, which increases the risk of hyperphosphatemia in patients with renal failure.

options.text: Fosphenytoin displaces phenytoin from protein-binding sites
Causes hyperphosphatemia in renal failure patients
ECG monitoring is not required when administering IV

question: Which of the following is an incorrect statement regarding fosphenytoin?

explanationHtml:
Phenytoin causes hypocalcemia and hyperglycemia rather than hypercalcemia or hypoglycemia.

  • Hypocalcemia and osteomalacia: Osteomalacia, associated with phenytoin use, characterised by hypocalcemia and raised alkaline phosphatase levels, is largely attributed to altered vitamin D metabolism and impaired intestinal calcium absorption.
  • Hyperglycemia: Phenytoin can inhibit insulin secretion, potentially leading to hyperglycemia and glycosuria.
  • Cutaneous pseudolymphoma: Long-term therapy may also cause cutaneous pseudolymphoma, typically T-cell predominant.
question:
A patient presenting to the ER with generalised tonic-clonic seizures is started on phenytoin therapy. All of the following adverse effects can be expected in this patient, except?

  1. Lymphadenopathy
  2. Ataxia
  3. Hypercalcemia
  4. Hirsutism
  5. Hypoglycemia

explanationHtml:
A newborn exposed to phenytoin in utero may develop fetal hydantoin syndrome, which can include features such as digital hypoplasia, microcephaly, and cleft lip/palate. However, gingival (gum) hyperplasia is not expected at birth.

Gum hyperplasia, due to overgrowth of the gingival collagen fibres, is the most common adverse effect of phenytoin in children and young adolescents on chronic use. It can be minimised by good oral hygiene.

Features of fetal hydantoin syndrome are:

  • Microcephaly
  • Digital hypoplasia
  • Cleft lip/ cleft palate
  • Craniofacial anomalies (such as an upturned nose, midfacial hypoplasia, and a long upper lip with a thin vermilion border)
  • Developmental delay
  • Cardiac anomalies: Ventricular septal defect, atrial septal defect, coarctation of the aorta
  • Growth deficiency

[[figure-1]]
question: Which of the following features would you not expect to find in a baby born to a woman on phenytoin therapy?

explanationHtml:
Hypersensitivity reaction to phenytoin warrants discontinuation of the drug. Switching to sodium valproate is the most appropriate course of action for this patient.

Sodium valproate is one of the first-line agents indicated for GTCS. Clonazepam and ethosuximide are primarily used in absence seizures and are not indicated for GTCS.

Clonazepam is indicated as adjunctive therapy in the absence seizures when first-line agents (ethosuximide, sodium valproate, lamotrigine) fail to control the seizures adequately.

options.text: Stop and restart phenytoin sodium after two weeks

question: A patient with recent-onset primary generalized epilepsy develops a skin reaction due to phenytoin sodium. What is the most appropriate course of action?

explanationHtml:
The clinical features in this patient are suggestive of a diagnosis of trigeminal neuralgia, and carbamazepine is the most effective agent for its treatment.

Trigeminal neuralgia is a condition characterised by excruciating paroxysmal pain in the lips, gums, cheek, or chin. It is commonly seen in middle-aged and elderly individuals. The pain may occur spontaneously or after movements like chewing, speaking, and smiling. Certain trigger zones are present on the face, which provoke these attacks. Tactile stimuli, such as washing the face and brushing teeth, may trigger the pain. The pain usually lasts for a few seconds to 1-2 minutes.

Carbamazepine is the first-line drug in the management of patients with trigeminal neuralgia.

Other options:

Options A and D: If carbamazepine is ineffective, then second-line agents like lamotrigine and phenytoin are used.

Option C: Sodium valproate, although effective for trigeminal neuralgia, lacks enough evidence for use.
question: A 51-year-old male complains of severe, sharp, piercing intermittent electrical shock-like pain sensation on the left side of his face. The pain was triggered by talking, washing his face, eating, and brushing his teeth. Which of the following drugs is most effective to treat this patient?

correctAnswer: A. It is indicated in focal seizures with impaired awareness
explanationHtml:
Carbamazepine is indicated for focal seizures with impaired awareness.

Carbamazepine is an antiepileptic drug that acts by prolonging the inactivated state of the Na+ channel, similar to phenytoin. It is used in:

  • Focal seizures with impaired awareness
  • Focal seizures with intact awareness
  • Generalized tonic-clonic seizures
  • Trigeminal and related neuralgias
  • Manic depressive psychosis.

Other options:

Option B: Carbamazepine is an enzyme inducer. It is a substrate as well as an inducer of CYP3A4 and CYP2C9.

Option C: Carbamazepine causes hyponatremia and not hypernatremia. Other side effects of carbamazepine include agranulocytosis or aplastic anemia, hepatotoxicity, water retention, and hyponatremia (by potentiating ADH action), and dose-related neurotoxicity.

Option D: It is not used in status epilepticus. Lorazepam is the drug of choice for status epilepticus.

options.text: It is indicated in focal seizures with impaired awareness
It is the drug of choice for status epilepticus

question: Which of the following statements is true about carbamazepine?

explanationHtml:
If carbamazepine is added to ongoing valproate therapy, it can result in hepatotoxicity.

Valproate undergoes hepatic metabolism, primarily via glucuronidation and mitochondrial β-oxidation. However, a minor but significant pathway involves CYP450 enzymes, particularly CYP2C9 and CYP2C19, which produce a hepatotoxic metabolite known as 4-ene-valproic acid.

When enzyme-inducing anti-epileptics such as carbamazepine, phenytoin, or phenobarbital are co-administered, they induce CYP450 enzymes, thereby enhancing the production of 4-ene-VPA metabolite. This enhanced production raises the risk of hepatotoxicity, so liver function should be closely monitored during combination therapy.
question: If carbamazepine is added to ongoing valproate therapy, what adverse effect is risked?

explanationHtml:
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) is not an idiosyncratic reaction that can occur after carbamazepine use. It is a dose-dependent adverse effect.

Hyponatremia can occur as a result of carbamazepine treatment and, in many cases, appears to be due to SIADH. This adverse effect is considered to be dose-related, with elderly patients being more susceptible. Therefore, it is advisable to monitor for signs and symptoms of hyponatremia and stop the drug once symptoms develop.

Idiosyncratic reactions to carbamazepine are unpredictable and hypersensitivity-related, like:

  • Rash
  • Stevens-Johnson syndrome
  • Eosinophilia
  • Lymphadenopathy.
  • Diplopia

Serious haematological toxicity includes aplastic anaemia and agranulocytosis.
question: In patients recieving carbamazepine, which of the following idiosyncratic reactions are not expected to occur?

explanationHtml:
Carbamazepine is expected to cause hyponatremia in this patient.

Carbamazepine potentiates the action of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). It can result in water retention with decreased osmolarity and hyponatremia, especially in elderly patients with cardiac disease, making sodium monitoring important during therapy.
question: A 70-year-old man is on carbamazepine therapy. Which of the following is expected to occur in this patient?

correctAnswer: D. Hyponatremia risk is less when compared to carbamazepine
explanationHtml:
The risk of hyponatremia with oxcarbazepine is higher when compared to carbamazepine.

The possible proposed mechanisms of oxcarbazepine-induced hyponatremia include either a direct effect of this drug on the renal collecting tubules or an enhancement of their responsiveness to circulating vasopressin, which promotes aquaporin channel migration to the apical membrane, thereby increasing water permeability. As a result, it leads to greater water retention, reduced plasma osmolality and decreased serum sodium concentration.

Other options:

Option A: Oxcarbazepine is a keto analogue of carbamazepine. It is a prodrug. The mechanism of action of oxcarbazepine is by blocking voltage-gated sodium channels (same as carbamazepine).

Option B: Oxcarbazepine does not cause auto-induction of metabolizing enzymes. It can induce CYP enzymes, but is less potent when compared to carbamazepine.

Option C: The active form is metabolized by glucuronide conjugation.

options.text: Enzyme induction potency is less when compared to carbamazepine
Hyponatremia risk is less when compared to carbamazepine

question: An 8-year-old child diagnosed to have focal seizures was initiated on oxcarbazepine. Which of the following would be incorrect regarding the agent being used?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of refractory seizures induced by hyponatremia caused by SIADH (due to anticancer drugs). Phenytoin is the drug of choice in this setting, as it can reduce ADH secretion and help control seizures by addressing the underlying severe hyponatremia.

Other options:

Options A and C: Carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine increase the antidiuretic hormone (ADH) levels, which increases the sensitivity of renal tubules to ADH levels and causes hyponatremia. Carbamazepine cannot be used in SIADH because of its antidiuretic effects.

Option D: Phenobarbital does not affect ADH secretion or action and thus will be ineffective in stopping the seizures.
question: A neonate diagnosed with rhabdomyosarcoma was started on vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and cisplatin. A week after initiation of treatment, the baby had multiple episodes of seizures, refractory to diazepam and lidocaine. Workup revealed an elevated ADH level and euvolemic hyponatremia. Which of the following drugs can be used to treat this patient?

explanationHtml:
The clinical features are suggestive of absence seizures, and ethosuximide is the most effective agent for this condition.

Typical absence seizures are characterized by sudden, brief lapses of consciousness without loss of postural control. There is no postictal confusion. The following subtle motor signs may accompany the episodes, such as rapid blinking of the eyelids, chewing movements, or small-amplitude clonic movements of the hands.

The EEG hallmark is a generalized, symmetric 3 Hz spike-and-slow-wave discharge that begins and ends abruptly, often provoked by hyperventilation. Ethosuximide works by inhibiting T-type calcium currents in thalamic neurons, thereby reducing seizure activity.

If first-line treatment is unsuitable, valproate or lamotrigine can be used, while atypical absence seizures respond better to sodium valproate.
question: A 5th-grade student, after receiving multiple complaints from teachers at school for repeated episodes of inattention, was brought to the OPD. The mother gave a history that her child had brief spells of staring that are not followed by confusion. Which anti-epileptic drug is the most effective for this child?

correctAnswer: C. Inhibits T type Ca2+ channels
explanationHtml:
The mechanism of action of ethosuximide is by inhibition of T-type Ca2+ channels in thalamic neurons at clinically relevant concentrations.

It also affects other ion channels affected including voltage-gated sodium channels and potassium channels.
question: A child with absence seizures improves after being treated with ethosuximide. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of this drug?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of absence seizures. Ethosuximide and valproate are the first-line drugs in this condition.

Absence seizures are characterised by sudden, brief lapses of consciousness without loss of postural control. There is no post-ictal confusion. The following subtle motor signs may accompany the episodes:

  • Rapid blinking of the eyelids
  • Chewing movements
  • Small-amplitude clonic movements of the hands

Hyperventilation tends to provoke absence seizures. The electrophysiologic hallmark of typical absence seizures is a generalised, symmetric, 3-Hz spike-and-slow-wave discharge pattern, as seen below.

[[figure-1]]

First-line drugs include:

  • Typical absence seizures: Ethosuximide (drug of choice), valproate, lamotrigine
  • Atypical absence seizures: Valproate
question:
A 10-year-old child is brought to the OPD with a history of vacant stares lasting for about half a minute. The EEG shows a characteristic 3 Hz spike and wave pattern. Which of the following drugs can be used for this condition?

  1. Carbamazepine
  2. Valproate
  3. Ethosuximide
  4. Gabapentin
  5. Pregabalin

explanationHtml:
Sodium valproate is an enzyme inhibitor and not an enzyme inducer.

It is metabolised by CYP2C9/19 and is an inhibitor of CYP2C9 and uridine diphosphate-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT).

Other options:

Options A and B: Phenytoin and phenobarbital are inducers of UGT and CYP2C9, CYP3A4, and CYP1A2 enzymes.

Option C: Carbamazepine is an inducer of CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP3A4 and UGT enzymes.

Enzyme inducers Enzyme inhibitors

Mnemonic: CRAP GPS

Mnemonic: RED VICK
  • Carbamazepine
  • Rifampicin
  • Alcohol (chronic)
  • Phenytoin
  • Griseofulvin
  • Phenobarbitone
  • Sulfonylureas
  • Ritonavir
  • Erythromycin
  • Diltiazem
  • Verapamil, Valproate
  • Itraconazole
  • Clarithromycin, Cimetidine
  • Ketoconazole
question: Which of the following is not an enzyme inducer?

explanationHtml:
Sodium valproate has no action on the GABA transporter.

Mechanism of action of sodium valproate:

  • Prolongation of voltage-gated sodium channel inactivation, preventing the neurons from firing repeatedly and rapidly (Option A)
  • Inhibition of T-type Ca2+ channels and reducing the firing of T-type currents may contribute to the effectiveness of valproic acid against focal, tonic, clonic seizures and absence seizures, respectively. (Option B)
  • Enhancing GABAergic activity by stimulating glutamic acid decarboxylase (GABA synthesis) and inhibiting GABA transaminase and succinyl semialdehyde dehydrogenase (GABA degradation) (Option C).

options.text: Inhibition of T type Ca2+ channels

question: Which of the following is not the mechanism of action of sodium valproate?

explanationHtml:
Osteomalacia is not an adverse effect of sodium valproate; it is more commonly associated with phenytoin use..

Phenytoin-induced osteomalacia is characterized by hypocalcemia and elevated alkaline phosphatase levels and results from altered vitamin D metabolism and impaired intestinal calcium absorption.

The side effects of valproate (mnemonic: VALPROATE)

  • Vomiting
  • Alopecia (Option B)
  • Liver toxicity (Option C)
  • Pancreatitis
  • Rash
  • Obesity (Option A)
  • Anorexia
  • Teratogenicity (most common: spina bifida), thrombocytopenia, tremors
  • Edema
question: Which of the following are not adverse effects of sodium valproate?

explanationHtml:
Valproate is the drug used for this patient as it does not cause contraceptive failure.

Valproate is an enzyme inhibitor, and it inhibits the degradation of oral contraceptive pills (OCPs). OCPs thus have a longer duration of action and less incidence of contraceptive failure with valproate.

However, other antiepileptic drugs like carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, primidone, oxcarbazepine, and topiramate are enzyme inducers. They cause increased degradation of OCPs and hence lead to contraceptive failure.
question:
A 23-year-old female patient is admitted to the neurology ward for evaluation of GTCS. She reports that she has been on oral contraceptive pills for the past 6 months. Which of the following drugs would you prescribe to this patient?

GTCS: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures

explanationHtml:
The clinical features and EEG findings are suggestive of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME). The most appropriate drug for management is sodium valproate.

JME, also known as Janz syndrome, typically starts in early adolescence and presents as myoclonic jerks in the morning, which is often perceived as being clumsy or causing patients to drop things. It may also present as generalized tonic-clonic or clonic-tonic-clonic seizures on waking up and absence seizures.

The EEG pattern seen in JME is 4-6 Hz in frequency (slower than alpha waves, 8-12 Hz). The polyspike refers to multiple brief, high-amplitude spikes in a single discharge. Following a polyspike, there is a slow wave with a higher amplitude than the background EEG activity, as shown below.

[[figure-1]]

Valproate is considered the most effective medication. Lamotrigine, levetiracetam, and topiramate are also approved for JME. In patients with myoclonic seizures, which are refractory to valproate, clonazepam or clobazam may be added.
question: A 16-year-old patient was brought to the ER with bilateral jerking movements of the arms. EEG revealed diffuse, symmetric, bilateral 4-6 Hz polyspike and wave discharges with a frontocentral predominance. What is the most appropriate drug for this patient?

explanationHtml:
The above clinical scenario suggests essential tremor in this patient, and an anti-epileptic agent, primidone, is considered standard therapy for the same, alongside propranolol.

Essential tremor (ET) is the most prevalent movement disorder. It is characterised by high-frequency tremors (6–10 Hz), most commonly involving the upper extremities. These tremors are usually symmetrical and bilateral. These tremors manifest when the person is trying to do some activity and are typically exacerbated by stress and improved by alcohol. Approximately half the patients with ET have a positive family history.

In severe cases, patients may also exhibit intention tremor with overshoot and slowing of movements, raising the possibility of cerebellar origin of this disorder.

Primidone, a barbiturate derivative and GABA-enhancing antiepileptic, is standard therapy. It is also an enzyme inducer. Treatment is started at a low dose and slowly titrated to reduce adverse effects such as sedation, nausea, and dizziness. Primidone is also used for generalized tonic–clonic and partial seizures.

While gabapentin and topiramate may offer some benefit in ET, they are not considered first-line therapies.
question: A 55-year-old man visits the neurology OPD with complaints of tremors in both his hands, which improve on alcohol intake. On examination, there is a significant worsening of tremors towards the end of finger-to-nose testing and head-nodding movements. Which antiepileptic is approved for use in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Gingival hyperplasia occurs in patients on chronic phenytoin therapy. It is the most common manifestation in children and young adolescents.

Gingival hyperplasia due to phenytoin therapy occurs due to tissue overgrowth secondary to altered collagen metabolism. The toothless portion of gums is not involved. It does not warrant discontinuation of the drug. It can be minimized by maintaining good oral hygiene.
question: What is the most common adverse effect of phenytoin in children and young adolescents on chronic use?

explanationHtml:
Eslicarbazepine acetate is an analogue of carbamazepine that has the advantage of once-daily dosing. It is a prodrug and is rapidly converted to active licarbazepine.

Oxcarbazepine is an analogue of carbamazepine that is also converted to licarbazepine, but it does not allow once-daily dosing like eslicarbazepine acetate.

Dacarbazine, in contrast, is not related to carbamazepine. It is a chemotherapy agent used in conditions such as melanoma and Hodgkin lymphoma.
question: Which of the following is a carbamazepine analogue that has an advantage of once daily dosing?

explanationHtml:
The drug of choice for severe or intractable Sydenham's (rheumatic) chorea is sodium valproate, as it doesn't have extrapyramidal side effects.

Sydenham's chorea is characterized by involuntary, purposeless, jerky movements that mainly affect the head and upper limbs. In the tongue, it is visible as the characteristic darting movements.

Medications used to treat Sydenham chorea are:

  • Mild cases - Providing a calm environment.
  • Severe cases:
    • Antiepileptic medications - sodium valproate (preferred), carbamazepine
    • Dopamine antagonists - haloperidol, pimozide
  • Severe, refractory cases - Steroids (immune-mediated)
  • IV immunoglobulins, plasmapheresis - limited studies, decreased efficacy (not currently recommended)
question: A patient with a history of mitral stenosis presents with the given intractable finding that is refractory to conventional therapy.  What is the drug of choice?

explanationHtml:
The first-line drug in the treatment of atypical absence seizures is sodium valproate.

The onset and cessation of atypical absence seizures are usually less abrupt, and motor components are more prominent when compared to typical absence seizures.

Typical absence seizure Atypical absence seizure
No change in body tone Change in the tone of the head and body
Precipitated by hyperventilation Precipitated by drowsiness
3Hz spike and wave pattern on EEG 1-2 Hz spike and slow-wave pattern of the EEG
Usually not associated with other syndromes Associated with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome
Absent or brief post-ictal state The post-ictal state is usually present

Sodium valproate is the first-line therapy for absence seizures in cases associated with secondary GTCS and atypical absence. Ethosuximide is the drug of choice for uncomplicated typical absence seizures.
question: What is the first-line drug for the management of atypical absence seizures?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical vignette of excessive hair growth secondary to treatment with phenytoin suggests hirsutism, and it is not caused by amantadine.

Amantadine, an NMDA antagonist and an anti-viral, used in the management of early, mild Parkinson's disease, levodopa-induced dyskinesia and influenza, is known to cause a cutaneous adverse effect called livedo reticularis, characterised by bluish discolouration of the skin. It is thought to result from the localised release of catecholamines, leading to post-capillary vasoconstriction, but does not cause hirsutism or hypertrichosis.

question: An 18-year-old girl was brought to the OPD with complaints of excessive growth of hair on her face and chest. She is a known case of epilepsy and is on treatment with phenytoin. Which of the following drugs would not cause this condition?

explanationHtml:
Perampanel is a selective non-competitive antagonist of the AMPA-type glutamate receptor. It is approved for adjunctive therapy of focal-onset seizures.

Other options:

Options A and B: Levetiracetam and brivaracetam act on SV2A proteins and modulate GABA and glutamate release.

Option D: Rufinamide acts on voltage-gated sodium channels.
question: Which of the following anti-epileptics is an AMPA glutamate receptor antagonist?

correctAnswer: C. Binding to synaptic vesicular protein SV2A
explanationHtml:
Levetiracetam has a binding affinity to the synaptic vesicular protein SV2A.

SV2A plays a role in vesicle recycling following the exocytosis of neurotransmitters. When levetiracetam binds to this synaptic vesicular protein, it decreases the release of the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate, thus preventing seizures.

Levetiracetam also inhibits N-type Ca2+ channels and Ca2+ release from intracellular stores. Thus, it is considered a broad-spectrum antiepileptic as it has an effect on multiple channels.

options.text: Binding to synaptic vesicular protein SV2A

question: Which of the following mechanisms of action is observed with levetiracetam?

correctAnswer: A. Slowly taper the drug over next 6 months
explanationHtml:
The mood changes observed in the above patient must be due to an adverse effect of levetiracetam. Abrupt stoppage of the drug can result in rebound seizures. So the best management will be to slowly taper the drug over the next 6 months.

Adverse effects of levetiracetam:

  • Somnolence
  • Asthenia
  • Ataxia
  • Dizziness.
  • Mood and behavioral changes
  • Psychotic reactions (rare)

Other options:

Option B: This patient is exhibiting mood changes, which are most likely due to levetiracetam. So it would be inappropriate to continue the drug.

Option C and D: Antiepileptics should be tapered off and changed, and should never be stopped abruptly due to a high risk of rebound seizures.

options.text: Slowly taper the drug over next 6 months
Continue levetriacetam since a 5 year seizure free interval is needed
Stop levetiracetam and start on a different anti-epileptic
Discontinue the drug as he is seizure free

question: A known epileptic patient on levetiracetam has been seizure-free for 2 years. But he develops agitation and anger issues interfering with his day-to-day activities as a result of the drug intake. Which of the following measures is to be taken next?

explanationHtml:
Tiagabine acts by inhibiting the GAT1 GABA transporter, thereby reducing its reuptake into neurons. It also increases the duration of inhibitory impulses in the synapse by prolonging the action of GABA.

It is approved as an add-on therapy for refractory partial seizures with or without generalization.

Other antiepileptic drugs that have GABA-enhancing activity are vigabatrin and stiripentol.
question: Tiagabine has been initiated as an adjunctive treatment for focal seizures in a patient. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?

explanationHtml:
Felbamate is the NMDA receptor antagonist prescribed to this patient. It also potentiates GABA action. It is indicated in refractory primary or secondary generalized seizures and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.

Felbamate is associated with aplastic anemia and liver failure.

Other options:

Option A: Memantine is an NMDA receptor antagonist that prevents glutamate excitotoxicity. It is approved for use in Alzheimer’s disease.

Option B: Riluzole is an NMDA receptor antagonist that prevents glutamate excitotoxicity. It is approved for use in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

Option C: Ketamine is an NMDA receptor antagonist that causes dissociative anesthesia and is used in general anesthesia.
question: A 25-year-old patient diagnosed with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome was prescribed a drug with NMDA antagonist activity. Identify the drug.

explanationHtml:
Ezogabine (retigabine) acts by opening neuronal potassium channels. Opening the K+ channels stabilizes the resting membrane potential and reduces the excitability of the nerve membrane.

The FDA recommends that patients on chronic ezogabine therapy need visual acuity and fundus examination every 6 months due to the possibility of retinal abnormalities.

Other options:

Option B: Rufinamide acts by prolonging an inactive state of the Na+ channel.

Option C: Vigabatrin is a GABA transaminase inhibitor. It is also associated with permanent vision loss and comes with a black box warning from the FDA. However, here the mentioned drug works on potassium channels, so this would be the incorrect answer.

Option D: Gabaculine is an irreversible GABA reuptake inhibitor that has only experimental value, due to high toxicity.
question: An antiepileptic agent that acts by opening neuronal potassium channels was prescribed to a patient admitted to the neurology ward. On discharge, the patient was asked to have a regular ophthalmological examination every 6 months. Which drug is most likely prescribed?

correctAnswer: B. Nephrolithiasis is not a side effect
explanationHtml:
Nephrolithiasis is a side effect of zonisamide.

Zonisamide is a broad-spectrum antiepileptic that acts by blocking low-voltage Na+ channels and T-type calcium channels. It also has carbonic anhydrase inhibiting activity that may result in metabolic acidosis and the formation of renal stones.

It is used in the treatment of focal seizures. Other side effects include somnolence, dizziness, headache, irritability, and anorexia.

options.text: Nephrolithiasis is not a side effect
Blocks low voltage gated Na+ channel

question: All of the following statements are true about zonisamide except:

explanationHtml:
Topiramate causes weight loss as one of its common side effects.

Topiramate has mixed mechanisms of action:

  • Reduces voltage-gated Na+ currents
  • Activates hyperpolarizing K+ currents
  • Enhances postsynaptic GABAA current
  • Limits the activation of the AMPA subtype of glutamate receptors.

Topiramate is used in focal seizures, GTCS, and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.

The side effects:

  • Cognitive impairment
  • Weight loss
  • Fatigue
  • Renal calculi

Sodium valproate, vigabatrin (highest incidence), and carbamazepine cause weight gain.
question: Patients on which of the following antiepileptic drugs will experience weight loss?

correctAnswer: D. Inhibiting the Ca2+ channel current
explanationHtml:
Gabapentin exerts its analgesic activity by inhibiting the Ca2+ channel current in this patient who is most likely suffering from post-herpetic neuralgia.

Gabapentin and pregabalin have close structural similarity to GABA. Still, they do not act through the effects of GABA receptors or any other mechanism related to GABA-mediated neurotransmission.

They inhibit the calcium channel current, which decreases the entry of calcium into the presynaptic neuron. When calcium entry into the neuron is reduced, there is a decrease in the release of glutamate. This lowers the excitability of the neuron, thus reducing seizure activity.

Therapeutic use of these drugs:

Gabapentin: Focal seizures, postherpetic neuralgia pain

Pregabalin: Focal seizures, postherpetic neuralgia pain, diabetic neuropathy pain, spinal cord injury pain, fibromyalgia pain.

options.text: Increasing the duration of GABA Cl- channel opening
Inhibiting the uptake of GABA at the presynaptic membrane

question: A 55-year-old patient presented to the OPD with complaints of pain over a healed dermatomal rash on his lateral chest wall. Gabapentin was prescribed to this patient. The analgesic activity of this drug is mainly exerted by which of the following?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario, along with hypsarrhythmia on EEG, is suggestive of West syndrome, a rare epilepsy syndrome of infancy. Vigabatrin is an inhibitor of the GABA transaminase that can be used in this condition.

Inhibition of the enzyme GABA transaminase leads to an increase in the concentration of GABA in the synaptic cleft, which is an inhibitory neurotransmitter. This contributes to its anticonvulsant property of vigabatrin.

West syndrome is characterized by a triad of:

  • Infantile seizures (also called salaam spells)
  • Developmental regression
  • Hypsarrhythmia, i.e, Himalayan wave pattern on EEG

The drug of choice in the treatment of infantile spasms or West syndrome is adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). The mechanism of action of ACTH or glucocorticoids is unknown but may involve a reduction in inflammatory processes. Vigabatrin is used if the spasms are associated with tuberous sclerosis.

Other antiseizure medications that may be helpful are valproate, topiramate, zonisamide, or benzodiazepines.
question: An infant presents with sudden jerky movements of the head, neck and arms. On EEG evaluation, a characteristic pattern of hypsarrhythmia is observed. Which is the GABA transaminase inhibitor approved for the treatment of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Vigabatrin is associated with progressive and permanent visual loss, primarily as bilateral concentric peripheral field defects.

It is a GABA transaminase inhibitor indicated in:

  • West syndrome associated with tuberous sclerosis
  • Refractory focal seizures with impaired awareness.

Regular visual field monitoring is recommended during therapy.

Lorazepam is less lipophilic than diazepam, has a lower volume of distribution, and has a longer cerebral half-life, thus making it preferable to diazepam. If patients do not respond to lorazepam, then other benzodiazepines can be used.

Status epilepticus refers to continuous seizures or repetitive, discrete seizures with impaired consciousness in the interictal period. For practical purposes, it is defined as any one of the following:

question: A 22-year-old female is brought to the casualty with seizures for the past 10 minutes. History from relatives suggests no seizure-free intervals in the past 10 minutes. After stabilizing the vitals of the patient, which is the first drug you administer to the patient?

correctAnswer: B. Immediately stop antiepileptics once pregnancy is detected
explanationHtml:
Stopping antiepileptics abruptly once pregnancy is detected in this patient is not recommended. If this is done, then there is a risk of uncontrolled seizures to the fetus, which can result in anoxia and intellectual disability. Antiepileptics have to be continued, and then the dose can be tapered slowly if there are no episodes of seizures.

Management of seizures in pregnancy:

  • If the patient is a known case of seizures and is on any antiepileptic drug, the same prescribed drug is continued
  • If the first episode occurs during pregnancy, the preferred drug is either lamotrigine or levetiracetam
  • Folic acid (1-4 mg/day) should be given to all

No antiepileptic is deemed safe in pregnancy. So, it is important to have the patient on monotherapy at the lowest effective dose, especially during the first trimester.

question: A 25-year-old female patient comes to the OPD with a positive urine pregnancy test. Her history is suggestive of antiepileptic use for 8 years. Which of the following statements is incorrect about further management in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The above illustration is suggestive of an infant with spina bifida of the open type, which is the most common teratogenic effect of sodium valproate.

Valproate leads to neural tube defects as it affects folate absorption. Thus, pregnancy is a contraindication for the use of valproate.

Other options:

Option A: Phenytoin is usually associated with fetal hydantoin syndrome.

Option B: Topiramate has shown growth defects in animal studies, and hypospadias have been shown in the male fetus, but the definite relationship is lacking.

Option D: Phenobarbital has teratogenic effects similar to phenytoin.
question: An infant is born with a birth defect as shown in the image below. It is the most common teratogenic effect of:

explanationHtml:
The drug of choice for juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) in pregnancy is levetiracetam.

Lamotrigine or levetiracetam are alternative first-line medications in pregnancy as they have fewer teratogenic effects. The drug of choice for JME, however, is valproate. In pregnant women or women of childbearing age, valproate should be avoided because of the increased risks of fetal malformations and neurodevelopmental delay.

Carbamazepine, vigabatrin, and phenytoin are not indicated in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy as they may worsen myoclonic jerks and absence seizures.
question: Which is the treatment of choice for juvenile myoclonic epilepsy in pregnancy?

correctAnswer: B. Continue valproate with serial drug monitoring
explanationHtml:
In the given scenario, since the patient has presented at 4 months of gestation, there is no benefit in removing valproate. This patient should be advised to continue valproate, and serial drug monitoring should be done.

Valproate has a high teratogenic potential. In patients with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, if they seek medical help before conception, the best step would be to taper valproate and then introduce lamotrigine or levetiracetam. But for a woman who is pregnant and is already taking valproate, changing the drug is not recommended. The patient is presenting in the second trimester, when organogenesis would have been complete. Therefore, tapering the drug and introducing lamotrigine is not an option as precipitating seizures has a greater risk of fetal harm at this stage. (Option A)

Other options:

Option C: Carbamazepine is not indicated in JME as it may worsen the myoclonic jerks and absence seizures.

Option D: Adding additional drugs to stabilized doses may increase teratogenicity. So adding lamotrigine to valproate is also not a viable option.

options.text: Immediately taper valproate and start lamotrigine
Continue valproate with serial drug monitoring

question: A 29-year-old primigravida, at 4-months period of gestation and history of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, visits your clinic. She has been regularly taking sodium valproate and is now concerned about the medication possibly affecting her child. What would you suggest to this patient?

explanationHtml:
Vitamin K is recommended for prophylaxis in pregnant women who are on antiepileptic drugs having enzyme-inducing properties.

Antiepileptic drugs with enzyme-inducing properties:

  • Phenytoin
  • Carbamazepine
  • Oxcarbazepine
  • Topiramate
  • Phenobarbital
  • Primidone

They induce CYP enzymes that interfere with the metabolism of vitamin K. Deficiency of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors can occur in the newborn, leading to coagulopathy and intracerebral hemorrhage.

Although hemorrhage is uncommon, the mother should be treated with oral vitamin K, 20 mg/day in the last two weeks of pregnancy. The infant should receive an intramuscular injection of vitamin K (1 mg) at birth.
question: Which of the following is recommended for prophylaxis in a pregnant woman who is on anti-epileptic drugs with an enzyme-inducing property?

Lamotrigine is effective in Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and has the highest propensity to cause rashes in young children.

Lamotrigine is also associated with toxic epidermal necrosis and Stevens-Johnson Syndrome in some patients. The incidence of serious rash and other serious skin conditions is higher with lamotrigine than with other anti-epileptics provided in the options. The occurrence of rash warrants the stoppage of the drug.

Other options:

Option A: Topiramate is one of the drugs indicated for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. It has a very low incidence of rashes. It most commonly causes nephrolithiasis, mood changes, and weight loss.

Option B: Levetiracetam is also effective in most of the seizures present in Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. It can increase blood pressure in children < 4 years.

Option D: Vigabatrin is also effective in Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, especially as an add-on therapy. It can cause permanent visual field defects.
question: Which of the following drugs used for Lennox-Gastaut syndrome is associated with a serious skin rash?

Macrolides are the least likely antimicrobial out of the given options to cause seizures.

Antimicrobials associated with causing seizures:

  • Quinolones

Other groups of drugs that are implicated in causing epilepsy:

question: Patients receiving which of the following anti-microbial drugs are least likely to develop seizures?

explanationHtml:
Among the given drugs of abuse, the drug which is least likely to be associated with seizures include cannabinoids as they are being tested for the treatment of various types of epilepsy.

Drugs of abuse that are implicated in causing seizures are:

  • Cocaine

question: Which of the following drugs of abuse is least likely to be associated with seizures?

explanationHtml:
Lamotrigine is an anti-epileptic that is known to cause Stevens-Johnson syndrome in patients.

Adverse effects of lamotrigine include:

  • Skin rash
  • Stevens-Johnson syndrome
  • Dizziness
  • Diplopia
  • Sedation
  • Ataxia
  • Headache

Other options:

Option A: Phenobarbital is an antiepileptic that can cause sedation and respiratory depression. It is not associated with SJS syndrome.

Option C: Topiramate is an antiepileptic that is associated with adverse effects such as renal calculi, angle closure glaucoma in vulnerable patients, mood changes, and weight loss. It is not associated with SJS syndrome.

Option D: Ethosuximide is used for the treatment of absence seizures. The main adverse effects associated with this drug are sedation, dizziness, and vomiting
question: A patient presented to the OPD with a skin rash since 3 days. He gives a history of antiepileptic drug use for 2 months and is ataxic on examination. He is diagnosed to have Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Which of the following drugs are implicated in these adverse effects?

explanationHtml:
Children who are on levetiracetam have a higher risk of developing several behavioral side effects, such as aggression, hostility, and nervousness, compared to children who do not use levetiracetam.

These adverse effects occur much less frequently with brivaracetam, a newer related agent with a similar mechanism but better behavioral tolerability.
question: Which of the following drugs if used can lead to behavioral effects such as aggression?

Pregabalin is approved for use in fibromyalgia. It is also approved for use in diabetic peripheral neuropathy.

Mechanism of analgesic action:

  • Interacts at the binding site of the alpha, delta subunit of voltage-dependent Ca2+ channels
  • Correlates with decreased Ca2+ channel function and release of neurotransmitters
  • Decreased neurotransmitter release is associated with reduced neuronal hyperexcitability.

Other options:

Options A and C: Gabapentin and tiagabine are also useful in fibromyalgia, but are not approved for this indication and are used off-label.

Option D: Topiramate's efficacy is not encouraging in fibromyalgia and neuropathic pain.
question: Which of the following drug is approved for use in fibromyalgia?

The first-line treatment for infantile spasms associated with tuberous sclerosis is Vigabatrin.

ACTH is considered to be the drug of choice for infantile spasms that are not associated with tuberous sclerosis.
question: What is the first-line treatment for infantile spasms associated with tuberous sclerosis?

explanationHtml:
Typical or first-generation antipsychotics primarily act by postsynaptic dopamine D2 receptor blockade.

Other options:

Option B: The second-generation or atypical antipsychotics mainly act by blocking 5HT2A receptors, but they also have a weak D2 blocking effect.

Option C: Ropinirole and pramipexole are D2 agonists used in restless leg syndrome and Parkinson's disease.

Option D: Lorcaserin is a 5HT2C agonist that was used to treat obesity. It was withdrawn in 2020 as it was linked to increased cancer risk.

Antipsychotics Drugs
First-generation D2 antagonists
  • Chlorpromazine
  • Haloperidol
  • Fluphenazine, Trifluoperazine
  • Thiothixene
Second-generation

5HT2A and D2 antagonists

  • Clozapine
  • Iloperidone
  • Olanzapine
  • Quetiapine
  • Risperidone
  • Ziprasidone

D2 partial agonists

  • Aripiprazole
  • Cariprazine

D2 and D3 antagonist

  • Amisulpride

5HT2A inverse agonist without D2 binding

  • Pimavanserin

Histaminic H1 and muscarinic M1 receptors are blocked by most of the first and second-generation agents. This contributes to sedation and anticholinergic effects of antipsychotics.
question: What is the primary mechanism of action of typical antipsychotics?

explanationHtml:
Constipation and dry mouth are side effects of antipsychotics that have potent antimuscarinic action.

In contrast, the following adverse effects are due to D2 receptor antagonism:

  • Hyperprolactinaemia → D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway(Option B)
  • Affective flattening / worsening negative symptoms → D2 blockade in the mesocortical pathway(Option C)
  • Rigidity in neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) → severe D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway(Option D)

Apart from their action on D2 and 5-HT receptors, antipsychotic drugs also exert the following effects:
