question: Which of the following new drugs has been approved for the treatment of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis?

explanationHtml:
The antimicrobial therapy given to the other concert attendees is called prophylactic therapy.

The antimicrobial treatment initiated in a patient who is not yet infected or has not yet developed disease is called prophylactic therapy. The goal is to prevent infection in some patients and to prevent dangerous manifestations of infections in other patients. Examples include perioperative antimicrobial therapy, antimicrobial therapy in immunosuppressed patients, and pre-exposure prophylaxis.

Other options:

Option A: Preemptive therapy is therapy for an asymptomatic high-risk individual with evidence of infection.

Option C: Empirical therapy is broad-spectrum therapy in a patient with symptoms of infection but no microbiological confirmation of the causative agent.

Option D: Suppressive therapy is given to patients when the infection is controlled but not completely eradicated by the initial round of antimicrobial treatment. This is usually indicated for immunosuppressed patients.
question: A young man who collapsed at a concert was suspected to have bacterial meningitis. The other attendees of the concert were administered ciprofloxacin by the medical staff on duty. What is this kind of antimicrobial therapy called?

explanationHtml:
Heteroresistance occurs when a subset of the total microbial population is resistant, despite the total microbial population being susceptible on testing. The resistant subpopulation is usually well below the assay-detection limits.

Heteroresistance represents gene alterations that occur due to the normal mutation rate in bacteria (about 1 in 105 or 106 colonies). Heteroresistant S. aureus (to vancomycin) and M. tuberculosis (to isoniazid and streptomycin) have led to therapeutic failures and mortality. C. albicans and C. neoformans with heteroresistance to fluconazole have resulted in increased treatment failures.

Note: In viruses, the resistant viral species that occur due to replication errors are termed 'quasi-species'. Quasi-species resistant to antiretroviral agents have resulted in antiretroviral therapy failure.

Other options:

Option A: When bacteria develop resistance to a single antibiotic, they may also develop resistance to antibiotics they have never been exposed to. This is known as cross-resistance. It occurs when multiple antibiotics bind the same target or are involved in the same bacterial pathway.

Options C and D: Idioresistance and alloresistance are not relevant terms used in the context of drug resistance.
question: The total microbial population was found to be susceptible to antimicrobials on testing. However, a subset of the same population was resistant, which was undetected. What is this phenomenon called?

explanationHtml:
Aminoglycosides (Gentamicin) exhibit concentration-dependent killing and are preferably dosed once daily for maximum effect.

The inhibitory effect of some antibiotics depends on the ratio of their peak concentration and MIC (minimum inhibitory concentration). This is referred to as concentration-dependent killing. The period during which the concentration remains above MIC is not relevant for such drugs. Aminoglycosides, quinolones, and metronidazole have this property.

Time-dependent killing is the type of antimicrobial action seen when the inhibitory effect is dependent on the period for which the drug concentration remains above the MIC. Penicillins (ampicillin), macrolides, glycopeptides (vancomycin), and 5-fluorocytosine have this property.
question: Which of the following drugs shows concentration-dependent killing?

explanationHtml:
Transformation is the molecular basis of penicillin G resistance in pneumococci.

Streptococcus pneumoniae develops resistance to penicillins by altering penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) in the bacterial cell wall, the molecular target of penicillins. Point mutations lead to alterations in PBPs. Sensitive pneumococci acquire the mutated genetic material via transformation. Transformation is the uptake of DNA from the environment and its integration into the bacterial chromosome by homologous recombination.

[[figure-1]]
question: A patient with pneumococcal pneumonia could not be treated using penicillin G as the microbe was found to be resistant to it. How is this resistance mainly acquired?

explanationHtml:
The extrachromosomal DNA present in bacteria that transmits drug resistance is a plasmid.

Plasmids are circular DNA separate from the chromosome. They can be transmitted from one bacterium to another by conjugation. They are usually involved in the horizontal transfer of drug resistance genes in bacteria. An example includes the acquisition of colistin resistance by E. coli.
question: What is the extrachromosomal DNA present in bacteria that transmits drug resistance called?

explanationHtml:
Multidrug resistance is transferred through conjugation.

Multiple genes, each encoding for resistance to a drug, can be present in a single bacterial cell. Typically, such genes are present on resistance (R) plasmids. The main mode of transfer of resistant gene-containing plasmids is through conjugation.

[[figure-1]]
question: How is multidrug resistance transferred among bacteria?

explanationHtml:
Linezolid is an example of a primarily bacteriostatic drug.

Bacteriostatic drugs are those that inhibit the growth and reproduction of bacteria without killing them. Bactericidal drugs are those that directly kill bacteria.

Primarily bacteriostatic drugs Primarily bactericidal drugs
  • Sulfonamides
  • Erythromycin
  • Tetracyclines
  • Clindamycin
  • Chloramphenicol
  • Linezolid
  • Ethambutol
  • Penicillins,
  • Cephalosporins
  • Aminoglycosides
  • Vancomycin
  • Polypeptides
  • Ciprofloxacin
  • Rifampin
  • Metronidazole
  • Isoniazid
  • Cotrimoxazole
  • Pyrazinamide
question: An example of a bacteriostatic drug is ______

explanationHtml:
Tigecycline is not a bactericidal drug.

Tigecycline belongs to a new class of glycylcyclines, which is a congener of tetracycline. It is a protein synthesis inhibitor and is generally considered a bacteriostatic drug. Isoniazid, daptomycin, and ciprofloxacin are all bactericidal agents.
question: You want to prescribe a bactericidal drug to a patient having an infection. Which of the following drugs will you not choose?

explanationHtml:
Cefepime is an antibiotic that acts by inhibiting cell wall synthesis.

Cefepime is a fourth-generation cephalosporin. Cephalosporins act by inhibiting cell wall synthesis. Aminoglycosides, doxycycline, and erythromycin are protein synthesis inhibitors.
question: A patient developed a surgical site infection with Klebsiella, which is found to be sensitive to a cell wall synthesis inhibitor. Which of the following antibiotics is this likely to be?

explanationHtml:
Doxycycline is a tetracycline that acts by inhibiting protein synthesis. It is the drug of choice for cholera.

Doxycycline primarily functions as a bacteriostatic agent. It inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit, preventing aminoacyl-tRNA from accessing the acceptor (A) site of the mRNA-ribosome complex, and thus halting peptide chain elongation.

Other options:

Options A and D: Cefotetan and oxacillin are beta-lactam antibiotics that act by inhibiting cell wall synthesis.

Option C: Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone that acts by inhibiting DNA gyrase.
question: A patient has presented to your OPD complaining of vomiting and rice water stools. You decide to treat him with a protein synthesis inhibitor. Which antibiotic do you choose?

explanationHtml:
Nitrofurantoin is an antibacterial drug that does not act by inhibiting cell wall synthesis.

Nitrofurantoin is activated by enzymatic reduction, with the formation of highly reactive intermediates by bacterial reductases. These intermediates are responsible for the antibacterial activity of nitrofurantoin. These intermediates react nonspecifically with many ribosomal proteins and disrupt the synthesis of proteins, RNA, DNA, and metabolic processes.

Carbapenems (imipenem), monobactams (aztreonam), and cephalosporins (ceftriaxone) are beta-lactam antibiotics that act by inhibiting cell wall synthesis.
question: Which of the following antibacterial agents does not act by inhibiting cell wall synthesis?

explanationHtml:
Bacitracin acts on the cell wall by inhibiting the synthesis of the cell wall.

Bacitracin is a bactericidal polypeptide antibiotic. It interferes with the dephosphorylation of bactoprenol (lipid carrier), which carries peptidoglycan subunits outside the cell membrane to the growing cell wall. It can also alter the integrity of the cell membrane. Bacitracin is mainly active against gram-positive cocci and bacilli.
question: You are studying the susceptibility of Streptococci to bacitracin in the lab. What is the site of action of this drug?

explanationHtml:
Pyrimethamine is a slow-acting schizonticide.

Pyrimethamine inhibits malarial growth by inhibiting the synthesis of folate, by inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase. It is often used in combination with sulfonamides as they have synergistic activity.

The female anopheles mosquito inoculates Plasmodium species in the form of sporozoites into the human host during a blood meal. Sporozoites migrate to the liver and mature into hepatic schizonts. Hepatic schizonts are released into the blood in the form of merozoites. Merozoites in the erythrocyte transform into ring form and erythrocytic schizonts. Some merozoites in the blood transform into gametocytes.

Antimalarial drugs are classified based on their onset of action of schizonticidal function as below:

  • Fast onset of action
    • Artemisinin derivatives like artemether, arteether, and artesunate are the fastest-acting
    • Chloroquine
  • Intermediate onset of action
    • Mefloquine
    • Quinine
    • Proguanil
    • Lumefantrine
  • Slow onset of action
    • Pyrimethamine
    • Sulfonamides
    • Tetracyclines
    • Clindamycin

[[figure-1]]
question: Which of the following antimalarial drugs is a slow acting schizonticide?

explanationHtml:
Primaquine is gametocidal to all species causing malaria.

Primaquine is active against both the primary and hepatic stages and additionally also acts on hypnozoites. Thus, it clears both active and latent infections, making it useful for malaria prophylaxis.

Primaquine causes free radical damage to RBCs and is not recommended for patients with G6PD deficiency due to a risk of causing hemolytic anemia.

The drugs with clinically important gametocidal activity (against all species) are:

  • High activity:
    • Artemisinins
    • Primaquine
  • Low to moderate activity:
    • Chloroquine
    • Quinine
    • Atovaquone/proguanil
  • No activity:
    • Mefloquine
    • Pyrimethamine
    • Sulfadoxine
    • Tetracycline

[[figure-1]]
question: Which of the following is gametocidal to all the species causing malaria?

explanationHtml:
Doxycycline can be taken as prophylaxis by the researcher before going to malaria-endemic places.

Chemoprophylaxis against malaria for travelers:

  • If the duration of travel is less than 6 weeks, doxycycline 100mg is to be started 2 days before travel and continued for at least 4 weeks after travel.
  • In cases of travel duration exceeding 6 weeks, administration of 250mg mefloquine once a week, 2 weeks before travel, is advised. This regimen should be continued for at least 4 weeks after travel.
question: A researcher who was studying plasmodium species decided to visit a malaria-endemic place in Odisha to do his clinical study for 5 weeks. He is planning to leave after 2 days.  Which of the following drugs can be taken as prophylaxis before visiting the malaria-endemic place?

explanationHtml:
The most appropriate first-line drug for the treatment of malaria due to P. vivax is chloroquine.

P. vivax treatment recommendations are:

  • Chloroquine-susceptible infections: Chloroquine or artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT).
  • Chloroquine-resistant infections: ACT is the drug of choice, but quinine is used during 1st trimester of pregnancy.
question: Which among the following is the most appropriate drug for a patient diagnosed with P. vivax infection, assuming the parasite doesn't have any intrinsic drug resistance?

correctAnswer: D. P. vivax and P. ovale
explanationHtml:
Radical cure is required for malaria caused by P. vivax and P. ovale.

Radical cure means eliminating both blood-stage parasites and dormant liver forms (hypnozoites).In the case of Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale, malarial parasites have an exoerythrocytic stage (hypnozoites). In the exoerythrocytic phase, malarial parasites are found in the liver, which can cause relapse of malaria after clinical cure.

Therefore, they require radical cure by drugs acting on the exoerythrocytic stage. Primaquine is effective against the exoerythrocytic stages of Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale in the liver. Primaquine is administered for 14 days for a radical cure.
question: Radical cure is required for malaria caused by which of the following species?

correctAnswer: A. Radical cure of plasmodium vivax
explanationHtml:
Tafenoquine is used in the radical cure of Plasmodium vivax. Total eradication of the Plasmodium species, which includes the clinical curative and hypnozoites phase, is called a radical cure.

Primaquine and tafenoquine (an 8-aminoquinoline derivative of primaquine) have very high activity against the latent tissue forms (hypnozoites) of the species. It is primarily used for the chemoprophylaxis and radical cure of P. vivax and P. ovale infections.

options.text: Treatment of malaria in children &lt;2 years

question: Tafenoquine is used in which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
Chloroquine is used in the treatment of systemic lupus erythematosus, porphyria cutanea tarda, and giardiasis, due to its anti-inflammatory properties, but it is not used in the treatment of Sjogren's Syndrome.

Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine concentrate in lysosomes and have an anti-inflammatory effect. It also has antihistaminic and antiarrhythmic properties.

Non-antimalarial uses of chloroquine are:

  • Hepatic amoebiasis
  • Giardiasis
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus
  • Discoid lupus erythematosus
  • Porphyria cutanea tarda
  • Severe polymorphous light eruption

Note: Chloroquine can be used to treat porphyria cutanea tarda, but in a very low dose (125 mg twice weekly). However, a dosage of 250 mg/day can trigger a porphyria crisis, which can be fatal.
question: Chloroquine is not useful in the treatment of which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
The woman is in the 1st trimester of pregnancy. According to the National Centre for Vector Borne Disease Control (NCVBDC) guidelines, Falciparum malaria during 1st trimester of pregnancy is treated with quinine.

Worldwide, most species of Falciparum malaria are resistant to chloroquine. In the first trimester, pregnant women diagnosed with uncomplicated malaria caused by chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum infection can be treated with quinine or a combination of quinine plus clindamycin. In the second and third trimesters, area-specific ACT is given as treatment.

Other options:

Option B: Doxycycline is useful in the treatment of malaria, but is not used in pregnancy.

Option C: According to the 2025 WHO malaria treatment guidelines, pregnant women with uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria should be treated with artemether-lumefantrine during the first trimester, owing to its superior efficacy, minimal adverse effects, and significantly lower risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes. However, research about cost analysis is still lacking in many countries, and hence quinine monotherapy is also still recommended. In India, the NVBDCP guidelines are followed.

Option D: Antifolates are contraindicated in the first trimester of pregnancy. Therefore, ACT regimens containing sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine should not be used during this period.
question: A 26-year-old woman who is 10 weeks pregnant, comes with history of fever and chills. She is diagnosed with falciparum malaria. Which of the following drugs will you choose for her treatment?

explanationHtml:
The image shows ring forms/early trophozoites in erythrocytes, which are binucleate (double chromatin), and this is characteristic of P. falciparum malaria. This, with the unstable vitals and chills, and seizures, depicts a case of severe, complicated falciparum malaria, and the drug of choice in this condition is artesunate.

Severe complicated malaria is caused by P. falciparum and is characterized by hyperparasitemia, hyperpyrexia, acidosis, respiratory distress, bleeding manifestations, cardiovascular collapse, renal failure, and cerebral malaria.

As per WHO guidelines, all patients with severe malaria should be treated with intravenous or intramuscular artesunate for at least 24 hours. Once the patient recovers and can tolerate oral medications, oral ACT for 3 days is recommended.

Other options:

Option B: Quinine is the first line for falciparum malaria in pregnant individuals. Artemisinins have replaced all drugs as the first-line therapy for malaria.

Option D: Artemether is used only if parenteral artesunate is not available.

Note: Severe falciparum malaria = IV artesunate → stabilize patient → complete with oral ACT.
question: A 32-year-old man presents with fever with chills and seizures. On examination, his blood pressure was 70/50 mm of Hg and labored breathing was present. Routine blood investigations revealed Hb of 4.8 g/dl. ABG was done and the pH was 7.21. Findings in peripheral blood smear are shown below. Which of the following is the drug of choice in this condition?

explanationHtml:
WHO-recommended artemisinin-based combination therapies are:

  • Artemether plus lumefantrine
  • Artesunate plus pyrimethamine-sulfadoxine
  • Artesunate plus mefloquine
  • Artesunate plus amodiaquine
  • Dihydroartemisinin plus piperaquine

Artesunate + Quinine is not recommended as a standard ACT because:

Both are blood schizonticides, not a true combination for resistance prevention, and they do not follow the principle of combining fast-acting artemisinin with a longer-acting partner drug.
question: Which of the following is not a WHO recommended artemisinin-based combination therapy?

explanationHtml:
The artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) recommended by NVBDCP in the north-eastern states is a combination of artemether and lumefantrine.

NVBDCP guidelines for the treatment of uncomplicated falciparum cases:

  • North-eastern states: Artemether-lumefantrine-based ACT
  • Rest of the country: Artesunate-sulfadoxine+pyrimethamine

In the north-eastern states (Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, and Tripura), the presently recommended ACT for P. falciparum malaria is a fixed-dose combination of artemether-lumefantrine due to the recent reports of late treatment failures with the current combination of AS+SP.
question: You are posted in a health centre in Nagaland as part of your rural service and a patient is diagnosed with uncomplicated falciparum malaria. Which of the following artemisinin-based combination therapy is recommended by NVBDCP for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Loading dose is essential for chloroquine because of its property of high volume of distribution.

Chloroquine is distributed extensively in the liver, spleen, kidney, lungs, skin, and, to a lesser extent, brain and spinal cord. Because of extensive tissue binding, a loading dose is required for achieving effective plasma concentrations earlier in the therapy.
question: Loading dose is essential for chloroquine because of which of the following properties?

explanationHtml:
The drug described here is lumefantrine, and its absorption increases when it is administered along with fatty food or milk because it is highly lipophilic.

Lumefantrine is combined with artemether in artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT). This combination is contraindicated in pregnant individuals and in children weighing <5kgs.

Mefloquine, Chloroquine, Amodiaquine → absorption is not significantly affected by food, so no special dietary instructions are required.
question: While writing a prescription for a patient diagnosed with malaria, the medical officer instructed the patient to take a particular drug along with a high fatty meal. Identify the drug.

explanationHtml:
The case depicts neuropsychiatric adverse effects that are commonly associated with the use of mefloquine. The US FDA has put a "black box warning" for this drug due to permanent and serious neuropsychiatric side effects.

The CNS toxicity caused by mefloquine includes:

  • Seizures
  • Acute psychosis
  • Severe vertigo
  • Confusion or decreased sensorium
question: A patient who was diagnosed with malaria was initiated on treatment about 3 days ago. Now she presents with seizures and confusion. Which of the following drugs is most likely to have caused this condition?

explanationHtml:
The finding shown in the image is bull's-eye maculopathy, and chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine use are associated with this side effect.

Bull's-eye maculopathy refers to the ophthalmoscopic appearance of a central area of retinal pigment epithelial depigmentation surrounded by relatively normal retinal pigment epithelium, giving a bull's-eye appearance to the macula.

Regular ophthalmologic screening is recommended for patients on long-term therapy to detect early changes and prevent progression.
question:
The finding shown in the image below is seen as a side effect of which of the following drugs?

  1. Chloroquine
  2. Quinine
  3. Hydroxychloroquine
  4. Artesunate
  5. Lumefantrine

explanationHtml:
Quinine is not associated with hypertension. It is associated with hypotension.

Quinine is used in the treatment of drug-resistant and severe P. falciparum malaria. It acts against asexual erythrocytic forms but has no significant effect on hepatic forms of malarial parasites.

Other options:

Option A: Quinine use is associated with cinchonism, which manifests as tinnitus, visual and auditory disturbances, headache, nausea, and vomiting.

Option B: Quinine has a stimulatory effect on pancreatic beta cells and can cause hypoglycemia.

Option D: Blackwater fever is a rare type of hypersensitivity reaction to quinine. It presents with massive hemolysis, hemoglobinemia, and hemoglobinuria that may lead to anuria, renal failure, and death.
question: A pregnant patient with severe malaria is undergoing treatment with quinine. Which of the following adverse effects is not associated with this drug?

explanationHtml:
Hemolysis in a G6PD-deficient patient is more common with primaquine.

G6PD-deficient patients are highly sensitive to oxidative stress. They are at increased risk of hemolysis due to the oxidant property of primaquine. Therefore, before initiating primaquine therapy, the G6PD status of the patient has to be determined. Passage of dark color urine is an indication of hemolysis, and the drug has to be stopped if it occurs.

Quinine, chloroquine, and hydroxychloroquine can also cause hemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients, but the incidence is less compared to primaquine.
question: A patient who was initiated on treatment for malaria two days ago, now presents with complaints of passage of dark-colored urine. Hemolysis due to G6PD deficiency is suspected. With which of the following drugs is this condition more common?

explanationHtml:
Sulfasalazine is a sulfonamide that is not used topically. It is used orally in the management of ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, and regional enteritis.

Sulfacetamide is used topically as eye drops for ophthalmic infections.

Silver sulfadiazine and mafenide are used topically for the prevention of burn infections.
question: Which of the following is not a topically used sulfonamide?

explanationHtml:
Trimethoprim is a selective inhibitor of microbial dihydrofolate reductase. Dihydrofolate reductase is involved in the reduction of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate.

[[figure-1]]

Sulfonamides, on the other hand, are structural analogs of para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) that interfere with the synthesis of folic acid.

Sulfonamides competitively inhibit dihydropteroate synthase, the enzyme that is involved in the incorporation of PABA into pteridine (dihydropteroate diphosphate) to form dihydropteroic acid, which is an immediate precursor of folic acid. Thus TMP is combined with sulfonamides due to their synergistic action.
question: Trimethoprim is an inhibitor of which of the following enzymes?

explanationHtml:
Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine combination is used for prophylaxis and treatment of malaria caused by mefloquine-resistant strains of Plasmodium falciparum.

Sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim is used in the treatment of Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia.

Sulfadiazine-pyrimethamine is used in the treatment of toxoplasmosis.
question: Which of the following combinations is indicated for the prophylaxis of malaria?

explanationHtml:
Co-trimoxazole is a combination of trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole in the dose ratio of 1:5 (trimethoprim: sulfamethoxazole).

The antimicrobial activity of this combination is because of its actions on sequential steps in the pathway of synthesis of tetrahydrofolic acid, as shown in the image:

[[figure-1]]

Each agent alone usually exerts bacteriostatic activity. But when an organism is sensitive to both agents, bactericidal activity may be achieved.

Because trimethoprim is more lipid-soluble than sulfamethoxazole, it has a larger volume of distribution than the latter drug.

Therefore, when 1 part of trimethoprim is given with 5 parts of sulfamethoxazole (dose ratio is 1:5; trimethoprim: sulfamethoxazole), the peak plasma concentrations are in the ratio of 1:20, which is optimal for the combined effects of these drugs in vitro.
question: Which of the following options correctly describes the dose ratio of trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole in co-trimoxazole?

explanationHtml:
Cotrimoxazole is considered the drug of choice for Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia prophylaxis in immunocompromised patients, such as those who have undergone organ transplantation and HIV-positive patients.

Prophylaxis for PCP is given when the CD4+ T-cell count is <200/μL.

Other drugs that can be used for prophylaxis are:

  • Aerosolized pentamidine
  • Dapsone
  • Dapsone plus pyrimethamine
  • Atovoquone
question: Which of the following is the drug of choice for Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia prophylaxis in a patient who has undergone organ transplantation?

explanationHtml:
Co-trimoxazole is not used for the treatment of chancroid. The first line for the treatment of chancroid includes ceftriaxone, azithromycin, erythromycin, and ciprofloxacin.

Other options:

Options B & C: Cotrimoxazole is indicated in both upper and lower urinary tract infections and also in prostatitis.

Option D: Patients with severe nocardiosis are initially treated with a combination of cotrimoxazole, amikacin, ceftriaxone, and imipenem.
question: Co-trimoxazole is not prescribed in which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
Cotrimoxazole is a combination drug consisting of trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole, of which sulfamethoxazole is a sulfonamide. Sulphonamides displace bilirubin from plasma albumin, leading to an elevation of serum bilirubin levels.

These drugs can cross the placenta and are secreted in milk and can therefore cause kernicterus in newborn infants if they are given to pregnant women near term or during lactation.
question: An infant had a serum bilirubin level of 33 mg/dL. The mother might have taken which of the following drugs during the third trimester for this to occur?

explanationHtml:
The given neurovisceral symptoms following the use of sulfonamides point towards a diagnosis of acute intermittent porphyria (AIP).

AIP is a rare heme biosynthesis disorder due to a partial deficiency of the enzyme porphobilinogen deaminase (PBGD). Diagnosis is made based on elevated urine PBG levels. Alcohol, infections, pregnancy, and certain medications can trigger attacks by inducing heme synthesis. This results in the accumulation of porphyrin precursors, causing symptoms.

Side effects of sulfonamides are:

  • Acute intermittent porphyria - sulphonamides precipitate attacks
  • Hypersensitivity reaction - urticaria, erythema nodosum, erythema multiforme of the Stevens-Johnson type, exfoliative dermatitis, and photosensitivity
  • Crystalluria - due to low solubility. It is treated with good hydration and alkalization of urine
  • Hemolysis in G-6-PD deficiency (sulphonamides are oxidizers)
  • Kernicterus in the newborn (displaced bilirubin)
question: A girl presents to the emergency room with severe abdominal pain, dark-colored urine, and seizures. You find out that she was recently prescribed co-trimoxazole for a UTI. What is the probable diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase enzyme
explanationHtml:
Fluoroquinolones inhibit two essential type II topoisomerases, DNA gyrase (in gram-negative bacteria) and topoisomerase IV (in gram-positive bacteria).

DNA gyrase introduces negative supercoils and thereby reduces the torsional strain that occurs when double-stranded DNA is being unwound for replication or translation. Topoisomerases IV are responsible for unlinking daughter chromosomes after replication. Quinolone antibiotics form a complex with the topoisomerase enzyme and the DNA, and thereby block DNA replication and bacterial cell division.
question: What is the mechanism of action of fluoroquinolones in gram-negative bacteria?

explanationHtml:
Levofloxacin has the maximum bioavailability among the given options.

While most quinolones are well absorbed, levofloxacin and ofloxacin have the highest bioavailability. Hence, intravenous and oral doses are the same for these drugs and allow for single daily oral dosing.

The fluoroquinolones act by inhibiting the enzyme bacterial DNA gyrase, which primarily targets the gram-negative bacteria. It nicks the double-stranded DNA, introduces negative supercoils, and then reseals the nicked ends. The enzyme topoisomerase is the major target of fluoroquinolones for gram-positive bacteria.
question: Which of the following fluoroquinolones has maximum bioavailability?

explanationHtml:
Ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin have substantial activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and can be used in this patient.

Mild to moderate respiratory exacerbations owing to Pseudomonas aeruginosa in patients with cystic fibrosis respond to oral ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin therapy.

Activity against streptococci is significantly greater with newer quinolones like levofloxacin, gemifloxacin, and moxifloxacin.

Moxifloxacin has clinically significant activity against anaerobes, including B. fragilis. It is reported to have similar efficacy to piperacillin-tazobactam for complicated intra-abdominal infection.
question:
A patient who is a known case of cystic fibrosis presents to the OPD with complaints of fever and increased cough with expectoration. Sputum culture is positive for Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Which of the following fluoroquinolones can be used in this condition?

  1. Gemifloxacin
  2. Ciprofloxacin
  3. Moxifloxacin
  4. Levofloxacin
  5. Gatifloxacin

explanationHtml:
Moxifloxacin does not accumulate significantly in urine and is not approved for the treatment of urinary tract infections (UTIs).

Moxifloxacin mainly undergoes hepatic metabolism, and very little of the drug is excreted in the kidneys, so it is not used in UTIs. UTIs are the only indication for the use of nalidixic acid. Ciprofloxacin and norfloxacin can be used in UTIs caused by susceptible organisms.
question: Which of the following quinolones is not approved for use in a patient diagnosed with urinary tract infection?

explanationHtml:
Delafloxacin is a newer fluoroquinolone approved for use in acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSSI) caused by susceptible bacteria, including MRSA.

Compared to other fluoroquinolones, which are zwitterionic in nature, delafloxacin is anionic. This enables the molecule to achieve increased intracellular penetration and concentration, especially under acidic conditions (skin wounds). This results in increased antimicrobial activity and a decreased adverse event profile at clinically potent doses.
question: A patient presents with a wound on his leg with purulent discharge. Pus culture was positive for MRSA. Which of the following drugs will you prescribe?

explanationHtml: Ofloxacin can be used in this patient as it is the fluoroquinolone that has high activity against M. leprae and is indicated in alternative multidrug therapy regimens for leprosy. It also has high activity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
question: Which of the following fluoroquinolones can be used in a patient with rifampicin-resistant leprosy?

explanationHtml:
Ciprofloxacin should not be given to this patient because it is a cytochrome P450 inhibitor and inhibits the metabolism of theophylline, which can potentially lead to theophylline toxicity.

Pefloxacin is another drug that inhibits the metabolism of theophylline and results in its toxicity.

Note: Asthmatic patient on theophylline → avoid ciprofloxacin or pefloxacin to prevent toxicity.

options.text: Ciprofloxacin decreases the effect of theophylline

question: A patient presents to the OPD with sudden onset abdominal cramps, fever, and diarrhea. He is a foreigner who is on a tour in India and is a known asthmatic on theophylline. You decide to start antibiotics. However, you would avoid ciprofloxacin in this patient because _______.

explanationHtml:
Moxifloxacin is metabolized predominantly by the liver and hence can be used safely in patients with decreased renal function without dose adjustment.

Fluoroquinolones, especially moxifloxacin, may be used as part of multiple-drug regimens for the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.

The kidneys primarily clear most available fluoroquinolones, and dosage adjustments are necessary in patients with renal failure. But fluoroquinolones such as moxifloxacin and pefloxacin undergo hepatic elimination and so should be used carefully in patients with liver disease.
question: A 52-year-old man diagnosed with multi-drug resistant tuberculosis requires second-line agents for his therapy. However, he is found to have a creatinine clearance of  50 ml/min. Which of the following fluoroquinolones can be started in this patient without dosage adjustment?

explanationHtml:
Among the following options, the most likely drug to have caused this condition is ciprofloxacin, since Achilles tendon rupture and tendinitis are side effects of quinolones and are predominantly seen in solid organ transplant recipients, patients on corticosteroids, and elderly patients (>60 years).

Fluoroquinolones inhibit topoisomerase IV in gram-positive bacteria.

Fluoroquinolones are used in the treatment of urinary tract infections, prostatitis, gastrointestinal, and respiratory infections, and as a second-line drug in anti-tubercular therapy. They are avoided in children and pregnant women.

Adverse effects of fluoroquinolones are arthralgia, tendon rupture, Clostridium difficile colitis, dysglycemia, prolonged QT interval, rashes, hallucinations, delirium, and seizures.
question: A 65-year-old man presents with symptoms suggestive of Achilles tendon rupture. He had undergone renal transplantation and is now being treated with an antimicrobial agent. Which of the following antimicrobials might he be on?

correctAnswer: C. Displacement of GABA from receptor
explanationHtml:
The clinical scenario indicates a drug interaction between fluoroquinolones and NSAIDs, resulting in CNS excitation.

Fluoroquinolones (including moxifloxacin) act as GABA-A receptor antagonists in the CNS. They displace GABA from its receptor, reducing inhibitory neurotransmission.NSAIDs (diclofenac) further potentiate this effect, markedly lowering the seizure threshold. The result is CNS excitation, presenting as delirium and seizures, especially in elderly patients.

options.text: Enhanced GABA binding to its receptor

question: A 60-year-old woman currently on moxifloxacin was brought in with delirium and seizures. According to her son, she had been taking diclofenac tablets over the counter to relieve her ankle pain, which had recently started. Which of the following best describes the reason for her current ER admission?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario describes QT interval prolongation (Normal QTc = 440 ms). Among the given options, moxifloxacin has the highest risk for causing this condition.

Gemifloxacin, ofloxacin, and ciprofloxacin have a relatively lower risk than moxifloxacin. Ciprofloxacin has the least risk for QT interval prolongation and torsades de pointes. Sparfloxacin has the highest overall risk of QT prolongation and has been withdrawn from many countries due to its propensity to cause torsades de pointes or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.

question: The ECG of a patient undergoing treatment with a quinolone is given below and you notice that QTc = 477 ms. Which of the following drugs has the highest risk of causing this condition?

explanationHtml:
Methenamine is a urinary antiseptic and is indicated in urinary tract infections. At pH<5.5, methenamine releases formaldehyde that inhibits bacteria.

Other options:

Option A: Galantamine is a central anticholinesterase approved for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.

Option C: Mecamylamine is a ganglionic blocker that can be used as an antihypertensive agent.

Option D: Pyrimethamine is an antimalarial agent.
question: Which of the following is a urinary antiseptic?

explanationHtml:
Phenazopyridine can be prescribed to this patient since it is a urinary anesthetic. It is used as a local anesthetic in urinary tract disorders to relieve the pain of lower urinary tract irritation, as in cystitis, urethritis, or prostatitis.

It does not have any antibacterial action but affords symptomatic relief of burning sensation, dysuria, and urgency due to cystitis.

Other options:

Option A: Methenamine is a urinary antiseptic, and at pH<5.5, methenamine releases formaldehyde that inhibits bacteria. It has no analgesic effects.

Option B: Nitrofurantoin is a antibiotic used in the treatment of UTIs. It however does not have intrinsic analgesic properties.

Option D: Phenacetin is an NSAID. NSAIDs are not used for pain due to UTIs. Additionally, phenacetin is no longer used in clinical practice as it was withdrawn due to risk of renal injury.
question: Which of the following drugs would you prescribe to a patient in order to relieve pain due to urinary tract infection?

explanationHtml:
The patient presented with fever, chills, and brown urine after starting a new medication. He was most likely prescribed nitrofurantoin.

Nitrofurantoin is a urinary antiseptic used against lower UTI caused by E.coli and enterococci. Its use results in brown urine. It is also associated with acute pneumonitis with fever, chills, cough, dyspnea, chest pain, pulmonary infiltration, and eosinophilia within hours to days of initiation of therapy.

The symptoms resolve quickly after discontinuation of the drug and are due to the drug being converted to highly reactive intermediates by bacterial reductases intracellularly. These highly reactive intermediates react nonspecifically with ribosomal proteins and disrupt the synthesis of proteins, RNA, and DNA.
question: A patient presents to the casualty with fever with chills and chest pain. He also gives history of passing brown-colored urine. He was prescribed an antimicrobial drug for urinary tract infection three days ago and his symptoms began after he had started this medication. Which of the following antimicrobial agents had most likely been prescribed?

explanationHtml:
Pefloxacin is mainly metabolized in the liver and hence avoided in patients with liver disease.

Quinolones with primarily hepatic metabolism include moxifloxacin, pefloxacin, and trovafloxacin, and have been withdrawn from the market due to hepatotoxicity. Quinolones primarily excreted by the kidneys include ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, norfloxacin, lomefloxacin, and ofloxacin. These are not associated with hepatotoxicity as much.

Other side effects associated with quinolones include tendon ruptures, QT interval prolongation, and GI distress. Quinolones are also potent inhibitors of CYP 450 enzymes and thus must be verified with the medications the patient is receiving to avoid drug interactions.
question: Which of the following fluoroquinolone is not given in liver disease?

explanationHtml:
Streptomycin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic, and the primary intracellular site of action of aminoglycosides is the 30S ribosomal subunit.

Mechanism of action of aminoglycosides:

  • Aminoglycosides are transported actively across the cell membrane into the cytoplasm (oxygen-dependent process)
  • The binding of aminoglycosides to 30S ribosomes causes misreading of the mRNA template and results in the incorporation of incorrect amino acids in the growing polypeptide chain
  • The resulting aberrant proteins may be inserted into the cell membrane, leading to altered permeability of the cell membrane of bacteria, causing bacterial death (bactericidal)

question: A patient diagnosed with tuberculosis is undergoing treatment with streptomycin. Which of the following is the primary intracellular site of action of this drug?

explanationHtml:
Aminoglycosides are rapid bactericidal agents.

Aminoglycosides like streptomycin and tobramycin cause hearing loss in a newborn child when taken during pregnancy. They are polar compounds and are usually excreted unchanged in the urine. They are distributed mainly in the extracellular compartment.

question: Which of the following statements about aminoglycosides is false?

explanationHtml:
Streptomycin is considered the drug of choice for the treatment of tularemia.

Tularemia is caused by Francisella tularensis, a Gram-negative intracellular bacterium. Other aminoglycosides like gentamicin can be used if streptomycin is unavailable, but streptomycin remains the first-line therapy.
question: A young man working in a rabbit farm presents with fever, lymphadenopathy and an ulcer on the hand and is diagnosed with tularemia. What is the drug of choice for this condition?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario suggests cystic fibrosis. Tobramycin, an inhalational formulation, is approved for use in cystic fibrosis patients with Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections.

Recurrent respiratory infections are the hallmark of cystic fibrosis, often necessitating the use of aminoglycosides during acute exacerbations. Tobramycin inhalation therapy is used in patients with cystic fibrosis who are chronically infected with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a common multidrug-resistant gram-negative bacillus.

It helps decrease the bacterial load without eliciting the side effects of systemic drug administration, improves lung function, and decreases the frequency of exacerbations.

Other options:

Option A: The injectable formulation of amikacin is used in cystic fibrosis.

Options B & D: Inhalational formulations of gentamicin and streptomycin are available but are usually not used.

Note: The question is about the approved inhalational formulation.
question: A child presented with recurrent episodes of cough with expectoration. Investigations revealed a positive sweat chloride test. Inhalational formulation of which of the following aminoglycosides is approved for use in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Amikacin has less activity against enterococci and hence is not indicated in infections caused by this organism. In enterococcal infections, gentamicin along with penicillin (or ampicillin) is given.

Aminoglycosides exhibit minimal activity against anaerobes and facultative bacteria under anaerobic conditions, and their efficacy against gram-positive organisms is limited; therefore, they can not be used as monotherapy for such infections.

When gentamicin is combined with the cell-wall active agents such as penicillin and ampicillin, a synergistic bactericidal effect is achieved. This combination is employed in the treatment of gram-positive enterococcal infections.

Amikacin is used against serious nosocomial infections caused by gram-negative bacilli that are resistant to gentamicin and tobramycin. It has good activity against most strains of the following organisms:

  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa
  • Klebsiella
  • Proteus
  • Serratia

Injectable aminoglycosides, such as streptomycin and amikacin, may still have a role in treating non-tuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) infections, particularly drug-resistant Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) and Mycobacterium abscessus.
question:
The organisms detected in culture and sensitivity reports of various specimens obtained from patients in a medical ward are given below. In which of the following infections would amikacin not be indicated as a treatment option?

  1. Pus culture positive for Pseudomonas aeruginosa
  2. Sputum culture positive for Klebsiella pneumoniae
  3. Urine culture positive for Proteus mirabilis
  4. Blood culture positive for Serratia marcescens
  5. Urine culture positive for Enterococcus faecalis

explanationHtml:
Due to its significant nephrotoxic and ototoxic potential, neomycin is restricted to oral and topical use; systemic or intravenous administration is strictly avoided.

Orally administered neomycin is poorly absorbed from the GI tract and is eliminated unchanged in the faeces. Oral neomycin can be used for the eradication of bacteria confined to the GI tract in the following conditions:

  • Pre-operative antisepsis for bowel surgery (statement 4)
  • Hepatic encephalopathy: To reduce deleterious ammonia-producing bacteria (statement 1)

Topical neomycin is used widely for a variety of infections of the skin and mucous membranes and to prevent infection of minor cuts and wounds. (statement 3)

Neomycin, often combined with polymyxin B, is used for bladder irrigation to prevent bacteriuria and bacteriemia associated with indwelling catheters. (statement 5)
question:
A 55-year-old man is prescribed neomycin as a part of his management plan. Regarding the clinical uses of neomycin, which of the following statements are true?

  1. Commonly used orally in hepatic encephalopathy
  2. Used intravenously to treat gram-negative bacterial infections
  3. Used topically for superficial skin infections
  4. Orally used for bowel preparation before colorectal surgery
  5. Used for urological bladder irrigation

explanationHtml:
Single daily dose aminoglycoside administration is more preferable to multiple daily dose administration because of the long post-antibiotic effect.

For certain classes of drugs, such as aminoglycosides and quinolones, their antimicrobial action is dependent on the peak concentration above MIC (Minimum Inhibitory Concentration). It is referred to as concentration-dependent killing.

High-dose, extended-interval dosing schemes take advantage of the concentration-dependent activity of aminoglycosides to achieve maximal initial bacterial killing. And then, because of the postantibiotic effect of aminoglycosides, a good therapeutic response can be attained even when concentrations fall below MIC for a substantial fraction of the dosing interval.

Therefore, a single daily dose would be equal to or more effective than multiple 8-hour doses. This dosing strategy may also reduce the ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity of these drugs. The graph below shows concentration-dependent killing:

[[figure-1]]

Time-dependent killing is an effect seen when the antimicrobial action is dependent on the duration, the drug concentration remains above the MIC. Beta-lactams, macrolides, and vancomycin have this property. The graph below shows time-dependent killing.

[[figure-2]]
question: A patient with hospital-acquired pneumonia is being treated with an aminoglycoside antibiotic by a single daily dose administration method. This method is preferred over the multiple daily dosage method because of which of the following properties of aminoglycosides?

explanationHtml:
Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic, and the peak concentration of aminoglycosides following intramuscular administration is achieved after 30-90 minutes.

Aminoglycosides need therapeutic dose monitoring because of their low therapeutic index, especially in patients in whom renal function is compromised. Both trough and peak levels are calculated for aminoglycosides.
question: A patient who was diagnosed with urinary tract infection receives a single intramuscular dose of gentamicin. Within how many minutes of administration is the peak concentration of this drug achieved?

explanationHtml:
Clinically, the most common cause of aminoglycoside resistance is drug inactivation by microbial enzymes.

The inactivating microbial enzymes are commonly acquired through conjugation and transfer of plasmids containing resistance genes, serving as a main mechanism of aminoglycoside resistance. However, amikacin is a substrate only for a few of these inactivating enzymes, making amikacin effective against many gram-negative bacilli that are resistant to other aminoglycosides.

Causes of aminoglycoside resistance are:

  • Drug inactivation by enzymes (most common)
  • Increased drug efflux
  • Decreased permeability to the drug
  • Modifications of the 30S ribosomal subunit that interfere with the binding of the aminoglycosides

options.text: Inhibition of transport across bacterial membranes
Drug efflux mechanism through the membrane

question: The urine culture and sensitivity report of a patient with urinary tract infection is positive for aminoglycoside-resistant Enterococcus faecalis. What is the most common mode of this resistance?

correctAnswer: A. A urosepsis patient with associated AKI
explanationHtml:
The dose of aminoglycosides is to be reduced in patients with renal failure (AKI) because clearance of the drug is reduced.

Aminoglycosides undergo minimal metabolism and are primarily excreted almost entirely by glomerular filtration. Therefore, renal failure decreases the clearance of the drug. Because the incidence of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity is likely related to the overall exposure to aminoglycosides, it is critical to reduce the maintenance dose and dosing interval of these drugs in patients with impaired renal function.

Other options:

Option B: Renal clearances are increased, and the half-life is reduced in cystic fibrosis patients, necessitating higher doses.

Option C: Burn patients have a more rapid drug clearance, probably due to increased drug loss through burnt tissue, and require higher doses in them.

Option D: Aminoglycoside dose adjustment is not required in liver disease

options.text: A urosepsis patient with associated AKI
A cystic fibrosis patient with acute pulmonary exacerbation
A diabetic patient with infected burn wounds

question: In which of the following patients will you prescribe aminoglycosides at a lower dose?

explanationHtml:
The scenario depicts a case of aminoglycoside-induced nephrotoxicity, and the least nephrotoxic among aminoglycosides is streptomycin because it does not concentrate in the renal cortex.

Nephrotoxicity from aminoglycosides occurs due to drug accumulation in proximal tubular cells, leading to mild proteinuria and the presence of urinary casts. A decline in GFR typically occurs after several days of drug exposure. The risk here correlates with the cumulative drug dose and the duration of therapy. High-dose, extended interval regimens are associated with lower nephrotoxicity compared to the traditional multiple daily dosing.

Among aminoglycosides, neomycin accumulates most extensively in the renal cortex, making it highly nephrotoxic and unsuitable for systemic use. In contrast, streptomycin shows minimal cortical accumulation, rendering it the least nephrotoxic in the drug class.

The other adverse effects of aminoglycosides, apart from nephrotoxicity, are:

  • Ototoxicity
  • Acute neuromuscular blockade and apnea
  • Hypersensitivity reactions (rare)
question: A patient who was on aminoglycoside therapy presents with nausea and vomiting. Investigations revealed rising serum creatinine levels, and granular casts were seen on urine microscopy. Which of the following aminoglycosides is least likely to cause this condition?

explanationHtml:
Vestibular toxicity is predominantly seen with streptomycin and gentamicin.

Aminoglycoside-induced ototoxicity results from the accumulation of the drug in the inner ear, leading to hair cell and neuronal damage. Patients receiving high doses or prolonged courses of aminoglycosides should be monitored carefully.

Ototoxicity with aminoglycosides is shown below:

  • Cochlear toxicity (high-pitched tinnitus as initial symptom) - amikacin, kanamycin, neomycin (Option A, B & D)
  • Vestibular toxicity (moderately intense headache and vertigo) - streptomycin > gentamicin
  • Both vestibular toxicity and cochlear toxicity - tobramycin
question: Vestibular toxicity is predominantly seen with which of the following aminoglycosides?

explanationHtml:
The scenario depicts a case of gentamicin-induced ototoxicity which is caused due to direct hair cell toxicity. Degeneration of vestibular hair cells and neurons leads to vertigo and associated headache.

Streptomycin and gentamicin produce predominantly vestibular effects. Amikacin, kanamycin, and neomycin primarily affect auditory function. Tobramycin affects both equally.

options.text: Inhibition of hair cell Na+/K+ ATPase

question: A patient who was recently started on i.v. gentamicin for enterococcal endocarditis presented to the OPD with complaints of headache and dizziness. By which of the following mechanisms does the drug cause this adverse effect?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario depicts the neuromuscular blockade effect of aminoglycosides, and tobramycin has the least potency for blockade in this group.

The maximum potential of causing neuromuscular toxicity is by neomycin, and the minimum potential is by tobramycin.

It is a recognised clinical side effect of aminoglycoside antibiotics, and this effect becomes significant (prolonged respiratory depression) when the drug is used in conjunction with neuromuscular blocking agents or calcium channel blockers. They are avoided in patients with myasthenia gravis.

Aminoglycosides cause neuromuscular blockade by interfering with calcium channels and thereby inhibiting acetylcholine's pre-junctional release and post-junctional sensitivity. The neuromuscular blockade produced by these antibiotics is not reversed by neostigmine but is reversed by IV calcium gluconate.
question: An elderly patient who was taken up for an emergency laparotomy showed prolonged respiratory depression which did not resolve with neostigmine.  On inquiry, the attendant confirmed that the patient was on aminoglycoside therapy. Which of the following is least likely to cause this effect?

correctAnswer: B. Binding to 30S subunit and inhibiting the binding of aminoacyl-tRNA to A site
explanationHtml:
Tetracyclines inhibit bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit, preventing aminoacyl-tRNA from accessing the acceptor (A) site of the mRNA-ribosome complex, and thus halting peptide chain elongation.

As a result, the elongation of the nascent protein chain is halted, effectively inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis. By disrupting this crucial step in translation, tetracyclines prevent the synthesis of proteins essential for bacterial growth and replication, ultimately leading to bacterial cell death or inhibition of further proliferation.

options.text: Inhibition of initiation of translation and misreading of mRNA
Binding to 30S subunit and inhibiting the binding of aminoacyl-tRNA to A site
Bind to 50S and inhibit translocation of peptidyl tRNA
Bind to 50S subunit and inhibit peptidyl transferase activity

question: By which of the following mechanisms do tetracyclines inhibit protein synthesis?

explanationHtml:
All strains of Pseudomonas aeruginosa are resistant to the action of tetracyclines.

Resistance to tetracyclines and derivatives is usually plasmid-mediated, and largely it is due to the ability of the gram-negative organisms to efflux tetracyclines.

Tetracyclines are active against MRSA and MSSA. Doxycycline and minocycline can be used in cutaneous MRSA infections. (Option A)

Rickettsia and chlamydia are highly susceptible to tetracyclines. Tetracyclines are considered first-line agents for chlamydial infections like nonspecific urethritis/ endocervicitis and rickettsial infections like typhus, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, and Q fever. (Option C)

Tetracyclines are bacteriostatic drugs that are more active against gram-positive bacteria than gram-negative bacteria. They are effective against spirochetes, Haemophilus ducreyi, Vibrio cholerae, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae. (Option D)

Note: Tetracyclines are also second-line drugs in patients with syphilis who are allergic to penicillin.
question: Which of the following organisms is resistant to tetracyclines?

explanationHtml:
Doxycycline is not preferred for use as a first-line in typhoid fever due to its resistance to gram-negative anaerobes. Third-generation cephalosporins (ceftriaxone), fluoroquinolones and azithromycin are more effective and hence preferred for the treatment of typhoid fever.

Enterobacteriaceae and gram-negative anaerobes are resistant to tetracyclines, largely due to the ability of gram-negatives to efflux tetracyclines. Hence, doxycycline is not used in intraabdominal infections. However, tigecycline has excellent activity against these pathogens and enterobacterials and can be used in the treatment of complicated intra-abdominal infections.

Doxycycline remains a first-line treatment for several infections, including:

  • Leptospirosis: Alternative to penicillin (Option A)
  • Lymphogranuloma venereum: 21-day course. (Option B)
  • Borreliosis (Lyme disease): first-line for early disease. (Option C)
question: In patients with which of the following conditions is doxycycline not used as a first-line treatment?

explanationHtml:
Tetracycline is used for the prophylaxis of cholera.

Tetracycline is the drug of choice for chemoprophylaxis of cholera and is recommended only for close contacts of a case of cholera. It is supposed to be effective in preventing the spread. Mass chemoprophylaxis for the entire community is not recommended.

Doxycycline in combination with rifampicin is used for the prophylaxis of brucellosis (Option B). It is also used in the prophylaxis of leptospirosis (Option C).

Note: The question is about the drug tetracycline and not about the class of tetracyclines as a whole.
question: Tetracycline is used for the prophylaxis of which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
Tigecycline is a glycylcycline, structurally derived from minocycline, and is designed to overcome resistance to classical tetracyclines. Its mechanism of action is similar to tetracyclines, binding to the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit to inhibit protein synthesis.

It is active against Enterococcus faecalis, Enterobacteriaceae, and gram-negative anaerobes, including strains resistant to conventional tetracyclines, making it the appropriate choice in this condition.
question: The urine culture and sensitivity report of a patient is positive for tetracycline-resistant Enterococcus faecalis. Which among the following is a minocycline derivative that can be used in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Demeclocycline, an antibiotic from the tetracycline group, can impair renal response to ADH, leading to nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. This unique effect is utilized clinically to manage SIADH.

It acts by reducing cAMP activity in the distal tubules, thereby blunting the kidney’s response to ADH/Vasopressin.

Among tetracyclines, this effect is unique to demeclocycline and is not seen with doxycycline or minocycline.
question: A patient diagnosed with the syndrome of inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) is prescribed a drug known to cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Identify this drug.

explanationHtml:
The drug described here is minocycline, as it is associated with vestibular toxicity, which manifests as dizziness, ataxia, nausea, and vomiting.

Symptoms of vestibular toxicity induced by minocycline are posturally related and usually occur soon after the initial dose is given and disappear 24-48 hours after drug administration is stopped.

Uses of minocycline are:

  • Cutaneous MRSA infections
  • Along with sulfonamides for nocardiosis (alternative therapy)
  • Subgingival administration in dentistry (extended-release preparations)
question: A patient develops dizziness, ataxia, and nausea after he was started on an antimicrobial drug. Which of the following drugs can be implicated?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario depicts a case of pseudotumor cerebri, and tetracyclines are associated with this condition in infants, even when given in normal doses.

Only elevated intracranial pressure is seen in pseudotumour cerebri, without any abnormality in the cerebrospinal fluid. Increased pressure returns to normal after therapy is discontinued.

Other side effects of tetracyclines are:

  • Teratogenic
  • Deposits in developing teeth and bones, causing brownish discolouration of teeth (chelating property)
  • Marked suppression of the normal flora of the intestine, causing superinfection. Pseudomembranous enterocolitis is a rare side effect.
question: An infant on antibiotics becomes very irritable. Investigations reveal increased intracranial pressure. However, the condition resolves on discontinuation of the drug. Which drug had the baby likely been on?

explanationHtml:
Doxycycline does not require dose reduction in patients with renal failure.

Doxycycline, minocycline, and glycylcyclines, such as tigecycline, have fewer renal side effects.

Antimicrobials causing acute kidney injury are as follows:

Acute tubular necrosis Acute interstitial nephritis
  • Amphotericin B
  • Vancomycin
  • Acyclovir
  • Foscarnet
  • Tenofovir
  • Penicillin
  • Cephalosporins
  • Quinolones

question: Which of the following drugs does not require dose reduction in patients with renal failure?

explanationHtml:
Loose green stools, vomiting and gray skin discolouration following antibiotic administration are suggestive of gray baby syndrome. It is associated with the use of chloramphenicol.

Gray baby syndrome is seen especially in premature infants. It develops due to the developmental deficiency of the enzyme glucoronyl transferase. This enzyme metabolizes chloramphenicol. Neonates also cannot excrete unconjugated drugs adequately through renal excretion.

The initial symptoms are vomiting, refusal to suck, irregularly rapid respiration, periods of cyanosis, abdominal distension and passage of loose green stools. Flaccidity, hypothermia, and ashen-gray skin discolouration develop after 1-2 days. Death occurs in about 40% of patients within 2 days. If there is a recovery, usually there are no sequelae.
question: A premature newborn was given an antiobiotic after birth, following which he developed vomiting, refusal to suck and passage of loose green stools. Over the next 24 hours, the neonate's skin turned gray. Identify the drug given.

explanationHtml:
Chloramphenicol acts by binding to the 50s ribosomal subunit, represented by site 3.

Chloramphenicol is a bacteriostatic antibiotic produced by Streptomyces venezuelae. It inhibits the binding of amino acid-containing tRNA to the acceptor site on the 50s ribosomal subunit. This inhibits the interaction between the peptidyltransferase enzyme and the amino acid. Thus, peptide bond formation and protein synthesis are inhibited.

Other options:

Option B - Antibiotics acting on the cell wall are beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, monobactams, carbapenems) and glycopeptides (vancomycin, teicoplanin).

Option C - Tetracyclines and aminoglycosides act on the 30S ribosomal subunit.

Option D - DNA gyrase is inhibited by fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin).
question: Chloramphenicol acts on which of the following sites in the bacterial cell?

explanationHtml:
Aplastic anemia is the most common blood dyscrasia associated with the use of chloramphenicol.

Hematological toxicities of chloramphenicol include:

  • Dose-related toxicity - Hypoplastic anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, or agranulocytosis.
  • Idiosyncratic response - Aplastic anemia (leading to fatal pancytopenia). It accounts for 70% of all blood dyscrasias caused by chloramphenicol.

Dose-related, reversible erythroid suppression is due to the inhibitory action of chloramphenicol on mitochondrial protein synthesis in erythroid precursors.

Chloramphenicol remains an alternative drug for the treatment of meningitis caused by H. influenzae, N. meningitidis, and S. pneumoniae in developing countries and also in patients who have a severe allergy to β-lactams.
question: A patient who was diagnosed with meningitis is on chloramphenicol therapy. Which of the following blood dyscrasias is most commonly seen with this drug?

explanationHtml:
Puromycin structurally resembles aminoacyl t-RNA and inhibits protein synthesis by premature termination.

Puromycin is an aminonucleoside antibiotic derived from the Streptomyces alboniger. It is comprised of a nucleoside covalently bound to an amino acid, mimicking the 3' end of aminoacylated tRNAs. It is incorporated into the C-terminus of elongating peptide chains and thus prematurely terminates protein synthesis. It is used as an antibiotic in cell cultures.

Other options:

Option A: Tetracycline binds to the 30s ribosome and prevents attachment of aminoacyl tRNA to the acceptor site of the mRNA-ribosome complex. It thus prevents peptide chain elongation. It does NOT structurally resemble tRNA. Tetracyclines have a nucleus consisting of 4 cyclic rings.

Option B: Chloramphenicol binds near the acceptor site of the 50s subunit of the ribosome. It thus inhibits the transfer of the elongating peptide chain to the amino acid-containing tRNA. It does NOT structurally resemble tRNA.

Option D: Erythromycin combines with 50S ribosomal subunit and interferes with translocation by interfering with translocation. Thus, the ribosome does not move along the mRNA to expose the next codon, and peptide synthesis is terminated.
