question: What is the mechanism of action of colchicine?

correctAnswer: B. Promotes excretion of uric acid
explanationHtml:
Sulfinpyrazone is a uricosuric agent that promotes the excretion of uric acid. It is used to decrease the body pool of urate in patients with gout. They act by inhibiting the organic anion transporter that is involved in uric acid reabsorption in renal tubules.

Uricosuric agents used in gout are:

  • Probenecid
  • Sulfinpyrazone
  • Benzbromarone
  • Lesinurad

Uricosuric therapy should be initiated in gouty patients with underexcretion of uric acid and when allopurinol or febuxostat is contraindicated or when tophi are present. Therapy should not be started until 2–3 weeks after an acute attack.
question: A patient with chronic tophaceous gout was prescribed sulfinpyrazone. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario and the X-ray showing Martel's sign point towards a diagnosis of acute-on-chronic presentation of gout. Indomethacin is commonly used in the initial treatment of gout.

In addition to inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis, indomethacin and other NSAIDs also inhibit urate crystal phagocytosis.

Other options:

Option A - Aspirin is not used because it causes renal retention of uric acid at low doses. It is uricosuric only at higher doses that are poorly tolerated.

Option C - Allopurinol is used for prophylaxis of gout.

Option D - NSAIDs are selected over colchicine because of the high prevalence of side effects with colchicine, such as GI distress and possible anaphylaxis.
question: A middle-aged obese man has presented to the OPD with acute pain around his left first metatarsophalangeal joint. He has a history of similar episodes in the past. X-ray is given below. Which drug is commonly used as initial treatment for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Rasburicase converts uric acid into soluble and inactive allantoin as it is a recombinant urate oxidase. It is more effective in reducing the urate level than allopurinol.

Recombinant uric acid oxidase is available as rasburicase and pegloticase. It is produced by a genetically modified Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain. They are indicated in gout only for chronic refractory gout. It is primarily indicated for hyperuricemia associated with tumor lysis syndrome.

Pegloticase is a recombinant pegylated uric acid oxidase that is indicated for the treatment of severe, treatment-refractory, chronic gout and also prophylaxis of gout.
question: A patient undergoing chemotherapy was diagnosed with tumour lysis syndrome. She was administered rasburicase. Which group does this drug belong to?

explanationHtml:
Allopurinol is recommended as the first-line urate-lowering agent in all patients with gout. It is a purine antimetabolite and an inhibitor of xanthine oxidase enzyme.

It prevents the conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid reducing plasma uric acid levels. Allopurinol is also a substrate for xanthine oxidase. The metabolite of allopurinol, called oxypurinol, is a non-competitive inhibitor of xanthine oxidase.

Other options:

Option A: Pyrimidine antimetabolite- Drugs in this class include 5-fluorouracil, cytarabine, gemcitabine

Option B: Colchicine is an inhibitor of neutrophil recruitment. It is not a urate lowering agent and is mainly used as an anti-inflammatory drug during acute attacks of gout.

Option C: Probenecid is a uricosuric drug. It is however not the first line drug for urate reduction.
question: You have prescribed the first-line urate-lowering drug to a patient with chronic gout. Which of the following is true about this drug?

explanationHtml:
Febuxostat is a non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor that is indicated for reducing hyperuricemia in chronic gout. Both allopurinol and febuxostat can be used as first line agents but since the question mentions a non-purine inhibitor is chosen, febuxostat is the answer.

Other options:

Option A: Allopurinol is a purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor.

Option D: Sulfinpyrazone is a uricosuric agent.
question: A patient was on treatment with indomethacin for gout. You decide to add a non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor to his treatment plan. Which of the following will you prescribe?

explanationHtml:
Lesinurad is a uricosuric agent.

It acts as an additional treatment for gout patients who, despite using xanthine oxidase inhibitors, are unable to reach the desired uric acid levels. It functions by inhibiting the reabsorption of renal uric acid through URAT-1 and OAT-4 transporters.

Lesinurad carries a boxed warning due to the heightened risk of renal failure and nephrolithiasis, particularly when administered as a monotherapy.

It is now discontinued in the U.S. and withdrawn in Europe.
question: A patient, who is a known case of gout on treatment with allopurinol, comes to the OPD for follow up. His serum uric acid level is 11 mg/dl. You add lesinurad to his treatment regime for adequate disease control. Which group does this drug belong to?

explanationHtml:
Pegloticase is used in the treatment of chronic gout.

Pegloticase is a pegylated uricase (urate oxidase). It catalyzes the enzymatic oxidation of uric acid into allantoin, which is a more soluble and inactive metabolite. It is used in the treatment of severe, refractory chronic gout or in cases where other urate-lowering therapies are contraindicated.
question: What is pegloticase used for?

explanationHtml:
The patient may have been given sumatriptan, a 5-HT1b/1d receptor agonist, which causes vasoconstriction and is used in migraine. Thus, sumatriptan will worsen angina by causing coronary vasoconstriction.

Angina will be worsened if the O2 demand of the heart is increased or there is reduced blood flow to the already ischemic areas. Triptans activate 5-HT1B receptors on vascular smooth muscle, causing vasoconstriction of cranial arteries which is the therapeutic mechanism in migraine headaches. However, they can also constrict coronary arteries, reducing blood flow and triggering angina or even MI in susceptible patients.
question: An elderly woman on treatment for migraine presents with chest pain. She has a previous history of angina/MI. Which of the following mechanism of the prescribed drug for migraine might have caused this presentation?

explanationHtml:
Statements 1, 2, and 3 are correct about drugs used in gout.

Gout is a metabolic disease associated with hyperuricemia. The drug of choice in an acute attack of gout is NSAIDs (non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) like indomethacin or the drug colchicine. Colchicine is poorly tolerated and should not be used in elderly patients with chronic kidney disease.

Indomethacin is commonly used in the initial treatment of gout. In addition to inhibiting prostaglandin synthase, indomethacin and other NSAIDs also inhibit urate crystal phagocytosis. (Statement 5)

Intraarticular steroids like triamcinolone or methylprednisolone can also be given.

Aspirin is not used because it decreases uric acid excretion. It inhibits renal tubular secretion of urate by blocking OAT1/OAT3 transporters. It is uricosuric at higher doses, which are poorly tolerated. (Statement 4)

correctAnswer: D. Calcitonin gene related protein (CGRP) receptor antagonist
explanationHtml:
Erenumab-aooe is a calcitonin gene-related protein (CGRP) receptor antagonist approved for the prophylaxis of migraine.

The pathology of migraine is not completely understood, but it includes activation of trigeminal ganglion nociceptive neurons and the subsequent release of CGRP from fibers associated with meningeal vessels. This is believed to mediate vasodilation and mast cell degranulation. Thus, CGRP is involved in the development and maintenance of persistent pain, central sensitization, and allodynia, which are events characteristic of migraine pathology.

Blockage of CGRP receptors by CGRP receptor antagonists causes inhibition of the inflammatory and nociceptive effects of CGRP at multiple sites within the peripheral and central nervous systems that are implicated in the underlying pathology of migraine.

Monoclonal antibodies that directly inhibit CGRP have also been developed. These include:

  • Fremanezumab
  • Galcanezumab

Note: The FDA has recently approved Atogepant, a calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) receptor antagonist for the preventive treatment of episodic migraine in adults. The recommended dosage is 10 mg, 30 mg, or 60 mg orally once daily. In severe renal impairment or end-stage renal disease, it is 10 mg once daily.

The image shows bull’s eye maculopathy, which is associated with hydroxychloroquine use.

Bull's eye retinopathy is characterised by pigment deposition in the foveola, surrounded by a ring of depigmented and atrophic retinal pigment epithelium. This is further encircled by a hyperpigmented ring.

Hydroxychloroquine is a disease-modifying drug used in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis. Both chloroquine and its derivative, hydroxychloroquine, are melanotropic. They get concentrated in the melanin-containing structures of the eye, such as the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and choroid. Significant retinal damage and visual deficits can develop in these patients. Therefore, baseline visual acuity testing and ocular examination are mandatory before starting hydroxychloroquine for a long duration.
question: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis has been on treatment for the past 15 years. During an annual eye check-up, her fundus appeared as shown in the picture given. Which of the following anti-rheumatoid drugs likely led to this side effect?

explanationHtml:
Methotrexate is the DMARD that increases extracellular adenosine.

It is a dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) inhibitor that leads to purine synthesis inhibition, and this is cytotoxic to lymphocytes. It also inhibits amino-imidazole carboxamide ribonucleotide (AICAR) transformylase and thymidylate synthetase. This leads to increased extracellular adenosine, which is anti-inflammatory. The increased extracellular adenosine is hepatotoxic and hence monitoring with LFT is needed every 2-3 months.

question: A middle-aged woman with rheumatoid arthritis was on DMARD therapy with a drug that increases extracellular adenosine. Which drug was she likely on?

explanationHtml:
The peripheral smear findings (with a hypersegmented neutrophil) point to a diagnosis of megaloblastic anemia. Folinic acid is given with methotrexate to decrease this side effect.

Methotrexate is a dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) inhibitor and thus can lead to a deficiency of folic acid, which may present as megaloblastic anemia. Folinic acid/leucovorin calcium/citrovorum factor is the 5-formyl derivative of tetrahydrofolic acid. Thus, it decreases the side effects caused by folate deficiency.
question: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis on treatment with methotrexate came for a follow-up visit. Her peripheral blood smear shows the following finding. What drug can be administered to alleviate this side effect?

explanationHtml:
Sulfasalazine can be used in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis as a conventional DMARD.

It is also used in the management of ulcerative colitis and regional enteritis. Sulfasalazine is metabolised into the following:

  • 5-amino salicylic acid (5-ASA) - It is not absorbed and is used to treat ulcerative colitis.
  • Sulfapyridine - It is absorbed and is used to treat rheumatoid arthritis.

It is used as monotherapy in mild cases and as an add-on drug in moderate to severe cases.
question:
Which of the following drugs is a non-biological DMARD?

(DMARD - disease-modifying anti-rheumatoid drugs)

explanationHtml:
Etanercept is a biological DMARD (disease-modifying anti-rheumatoid drug) that acts by TNF-alpha inhibition.

Etanercept is a fusion protein that combines the extracellular portion of the TNF receptor with the Fc portion of IgG1. It acts as a decoy receptor for TNF-α, binding circulating TNF and preventing it from interacting with its cell surface receptors. This reduces the inflammatory cascade responsible for rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, and other autoimmune diseases.

question: You are using TNF alpha inhibitors in the treatment of a patient with rheumatoid arthritis. Which of the following is not true regarding these drugs?

The IL-1 receptor antagonist that is used in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis is anakinra.

Anakinra is a biological disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) used in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis. All biological DMARDs downregulate the immune system and can lead to adverse effects like opportunistic infections and flaring of latent TB. Thus, before starting them, tuberculosis screening must be done. Anakinra can also lead to neutropenia, and hence, CBC needs to be done at initiation and repeated every month for 3 months, then every 4 months for 1 year.
question: A middle-aged man with rheumatoid arthritis on treatment with methotrexate presents to your OPD complaining of no improvement in his condition. Which of the following is an IL-1 receptor antagonist that can you prescribe for him?

explanationHtml:
The monoclonal antibody approved for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis is sarilumab.

It is an IL-6 receptor antagonist indicated for the treatment of adults with moderate to severe rheumatoid arthritis who show inadequate response or intolerance to one or more disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs).

Other options:

Option A: Durvalumab is an anti-PD-L1 antibody approved for metastatic urothelial cancer.

Option C: Nivolumab is a fully human monoclonal IgG4 antibody that blocks the interaction between PD-1 (Programmed Cell Death-1) receptor and its ligands.

Option D: Pembrolizumab (formerly called lambrolizumab or MK-3475) is a humanized monoclonal IgG4-κ isotype antibody that blocks the interaction between PD-1 and its ligands. Nivolumab and pembrolizumab are used to treat advanced melanoma.
question: Which is the monoclonal antibody approved for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis?

explanationHtml:
Baricitinib is a Janus kinase inhibitor approved for use in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. Upadacitinib and tofacitinib are also used for the same purpose and have the same mechanism.

Other options:

Option A: Ruxolitinib is a Janus kinase inhibitor, approved for use in various forms of myelofibrosis, polycythemia vera, and acute graft vs host disease.

Option C: Denosumab is a RANK-L inhibitor that is approved for the treatment of osteoporosis.

Option D: Dasatinib and ponatinib are BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitors indicated for the treatment of CML.
question: Which of the following is a Janus kinase inhibitor approved for use in rheumatoid arthritis?

correctAnswer: D. As monotherapy for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis
explanationHtml:
Glucocorticoids are not used as monotherapy for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis (RA).

Low to moderate doses of glucocorticoids may be administered as bridging therapy initially to achieve rapid disease control till DMARDs take effect, which may take several weeks or even months (option B). A burst of glucocorticoids for 1-2 weeks may be prescribed to manage acute disease flares (option A). Chronic therapy with low doses may be needed to control the disease in patients with an inadequate response to DMARD therapy (option C). High doses of glucocorticoids may be needed to treat severe extraarticular manifestations of RA. Intraarticular injection of triamcinolone can be considered for one/few actively inflamed joints.

question: Which of the following histamine receptors are presynaptic autoreceptors?

correctAnswer: B. Increase in H2 mediated gastric secretion
explanationHtml:
H3 receptor agonist decreases H2-mediated gastric secretion.

H3 receptors are presynaptic inhibitory autoreceptors on histaminergic neurons. H3 receptor agonists decrease the release of histamine and have actions similar to those of antihistamines.

Normally, histamine increases gastric secretion by acting through the H2 receptor in the stomach. H3 receptor agonist decreases histamine release and hence decreases H2 receptor-mediated gastric secretion.

question: A highway truck driver has presented with profuse rhinorrhea and sneezing. Which of the following drugs will you prefer to prescribe to him?

explanationHtml:
The scenario points towards a diagnosis of drug-induced Parkinsonism due to long-term intake of haloperidol. Promethazine is the preferred antihistamine as it has the strongest anticholinergic (muscarinic blocking) activity among the given options.

Drug-induced Parkinsonism is caused by drugs that have D2 dopamine antagonistic action, like typical antipsychotics (e.g. haloperidol)—the decrease in dopaminergic activity results in an unbalanced cholinergic activity. Anticholinergics act by restoring balance.

First-generation H1 antagonists have anticholinergic properties, while second-generation H1 antagonists do not.

H1 antagonists having high anticholinergic activity include promethazine, diphenhydramine, dimenhydrinate and pheniramine.
question: A patient presents to you with difficulty in writing and performing fine movements. On examination, he has a pill-rolling resting tremor. He has been on treatment with haloperidol for the past 12 years. Which of the following antihistamines would you prefer to prescribe to him?

explanationHtml:
Rupatadine is a second-generation antihistaminic drug that has additional platelet-activating factor (PAF) antagonistic properties and is indicated in allergic rhinitis.

PAF is an endogenous phospholipid-derived mediator produced by various inflammatory cells such as alveolar macrophages, eosinophils, basophils, platelets and neutrophils, released in response to allergic/inflammatory stimuli. It is involved in the pathophysiology of allergic rhinitis, asthma, and anaphylaxis.
question: Which among the following antihistaminic drugs has additional platelet-activating factor antagonistic property?

explanationHtml:
Azelastine is an antihistamine that has an intranasal preparation for allergic rhinitis.

Olopatadine and azelastine are the second-generation antihistaminics available as intranasal (nasal spray) preparations for allergic rhinitis. They have good topical activity. Azelastine shows mast-cell stabilising and anti-inflammatory properties, useful in the management of allergic rhinitis and as ophthalmic drops in allergic conjunctivitis.

Intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) remain the preferred monotherapy for persistent allergic rhinitis (AR). However, additional studies support the additive benefit of combination treatment with INCS and intranasal antihistamines in AR. For patients receiving INCS, an intranasal decongestant may be added to the treatment for up to 4 weeks.
question: A patient having persistent allergic rhinitis is on treatment with intranasal steroids. You wish to add an antihistamine to his treatment regimen. He requests an intranasal preparation. Which of the following will you prescribe?

explanationHtml:
Cyproheptadine, a first-generation antihistamine, also possesses 5-HT2 receptor antagonism, which contributes to its appetite-stimulating effect and has been used to promote weight gain in poor eaters.

This orexigenic effect may be attributed to its antagonism of serotonin receptors in the hypothalamus, involved in appetite regulation.

Other options:

Option A: Cyclizine, a first-generation antihistamine, has anti-nausea properties due to its anti-cholinergic effects and can also be used in motion sickness.

Option B & C: Azelastine and olopatidine, both being second-generation antihistamines, are used topically via intranasal or ophthalmic route for the management of allergic rhinitis or allergic conjunctivitis, respectively.
question: A patient with cystic fibrosis was found to be underweight during his regular check-up. He complains of low appetite, and you decide to prescribe an appetite-stimulating agent. Which antihistaminic drug can you prescribe to him?

explanationHtml:
The scenario given in the question likely points to a diagnosis of Meniere's disease. Betahistine is a selective H1 agonist used in this condition.

Betahistine is a structural analogue of histamine possessing H1 agonistic actions in the blood vessels of the inner ear, causing vasodilation and increasing capillary permeability, thereby reducing endolymphatic pressure. Hence, it is used to relieve symptoms of vertigo in Meniere's disease.

It also functions as a potent H3 receptor antagonist, increasing the turnover of histamine from post-synaptic histaminergic nerve receptors, subsequently increasing H1 agonist activity. It is also found to inhibit vestibular nuclei activity in the brainstem, decreasing vertigo symptoms.

Acute attacks of Meniere's disease can be treated with bed rest and vestibular sedatives like dimenhydrinate or promethazine theoclate (first-generation H1 antagonists), or prochlorperazine (a D2 receptor antagonist). Betahistine is used in chronic cases of this condition.
question: A patient has presented to your OPD complaining of hearing loss following an attack of vertigo. He says he has had similar episodes in the past. You decide to prescribe him betahistine. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?

explanationHtml:
Tiprolisant is a selective H3 receptor antagonist and inverse agonist used in the management of narcolepsy.

Pitolisant (formerly known as tiprolisant), a H3 receptor antagonist and inverse agonist, promotes wakefulness, improves cognitive functions (e.g., enhances memory, learning, and attention), and reduces food intake. It also reduces excessive daytime sleepiness and cataplexy in adults with narcolepsy.
question: A patient with narcolepsy has been prescribed tiprolisant. How does this drug act?

explanationHtml:
Promethazine is used for motion sickness. It is an antihistaminic agent that acts as an antagonist of H1 receptors. It also has central anticholinergic activity that is responsible for its antiemetic action.

It can be used for treatment and prophylaxis in the management of motion sickness.
question: Which of the following drugs is used for the treatment of motion sickness?

explanationHtml:
Aspirin at low doses (75mg) primarily acts by inhibiting cyclooxygenase 1 (COX-1).

Low-dose aspirin, used for antiplatelet action, results in selective inhibition of platelet COX-1 (thromboxane synthase), inhibiting its ability to form thromboxane A2 (needed for platelet aggregation). As platelets lack nuclei, new platelets have to be formed (life span of 7-10 days) for the return of COX-1 activity.

At higher doses (~1g/day), aspirin also inhibits COX-2 and results in decreased production of prostacyclin from endothelium. This may nullify the beneficial anti-aggregatory effect of aspirin.

question: A patient with a history of myocardial infarction has been on 75 mg aspirin OD for two years. The drug primarily acts by inhibiting which enzyme?

correctAnswer: A. It inhibits Gp IIb/IIIa receptors
explanationHtml:
Clopidogrel acts by irreversible inhibition of P2Y12 receptors of the platelets.

Eptifibatide, abciximab and tirofiban are GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors.

Clopidogrel blocks platelet aggregation for the entire lifetime of platelets. It is a prodrug and requires activation by CYP 2C19 to work. PPIs such as omeprazole and pantoprazole inhibit CYP 2C19, thus reducing the formation of the active metabolite of clopidogrel and leading to therapeutic failure.

Other options:

Options B and C: The onset of action is slow (starts after 4 hours) as it requires metabolic activation by the hepatic CYP2C19 enzyme. Patients with a loss of function mutation of the CYP2C19 allele exhibit reduced platelet inhibition and experience a higher rate of cardiovascular events.

question: A 55-year-old underwent coronary stent implantation. He was prescribed dual antiplatelet therapy for 6 months in which clopidogrel is one of the components. Which of the following is not true about this drug?

explanationHtml:
Clopidogrel is a prodrug that is converted into an active metabolite by the CYP2C19 enzyme and omeprazole can reduce the efficacy of clopidogrel due to its CYP2C19 inhibitory activity.

Other options:

Option B: Prasugrel is converted to its active metabolite mainly by other CYP enzymes, and therefore, omeprazole does not interfere with its activation.

Option C: Ticagrelor does not require activation and is metabolized by the CYP3A4 enzyme.

Option D: Vorapaxar is a thrombin receptor antagonist that is also metabolized by the CYP3A4 enzyme.
question: The efficacy of which of the following antiplatelet drugs will be reduced, if omeprazole is used concurrently?

explanationHtml:
Ticagrelor is not a prodrug and does not require metabolic activation to exert its antiplatelet action.

It is an orally active, reversible antagonist of the P2Y12 subtype of ADP receptors. Since the drug does not require hepatic activation, it can be used in patients with CYP2C19 mutations. Ticagrelor is metabolized into another active metabolite by CYP3A4 and is finally excreted in the urine.

Clopidogrel, prasugrel, and ticlopidine are irreversible antagonists of P2Y12 and are prodrugs requiring metabolic activation in the liver for optimal effect.
question: Which of the following is not a prodrug?

correctAnswer: C. It is contraindicated in cerebrovascular accidents
explanationHtml:
Prasugrel is contraindicated in cerebrovascular accidents as it is associated with higher rates of fatal and life-threatening bleeding.

This risk of bleeding is increased with concomitant administration of NSAIDs or SSRIs.

Other options:

Option A: It is an irreversible inhibitor of the ADP (P2Y12) receptor of platelets.

Option B: It has a faster onset of action and produces greater inhibition of platelets than clopidogrel.

Option D: Dose adjustment is not needed in moderate hepatic and renal impairment.

question: Which of the following statements is true about prasugrel?

explanationHtml:
Vorapaxar is a competitive antagonist of PAR-1 (thrombin receptor) and inhibits thrombin-induced platelet aggregation.

Abciximab, tirofiban, and eptifibatide act by blocking Gp IIb/IIIa receptors. They are used in patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for acute coronary syndrome. They carry a high risk of bleeding and can cause thrombocytopenia.

Eptifibatide is contraindicated in renal failure and tirofiban needs dose adjustment in cases of renal impairment.

question: Which of the following drugs does not act by blocking Gp IIb/ IIIa receptors?

explanationHtml:
Abciximab can safely be administered to this patient who is likely suffering from acute kidney injury (urine volume less than 0.5 mL/kg per hour for 6 hours). Abciximab is safe to use in renal disease as it is not excreted by the kidneys.

Abciximab, eptifibatide, and tirofiban are parenteral GpIIb/IIIa receptor antagonists used in the treatment of acute coronary syndromes.

Eptifibatide is contraindicated in renal failure and tirofiban needs dose adjustment in cases of renal impairment. Both these drugs undergo renal clearance and used cautiously in renal impairment.
question: A patient with a urine output of 0.4ml/Kg per hour in the last 6 hours can be safely administered which of the following GP IIb/IIIa antagonists?

explanationHtml:
Cangrelor is an intravenous, reversible P2Y12 (ADP) receptor inhibitor with rapid onset and offset, making it ideal during percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI).

Abciximab, eptifibatide, and tirofiban are parenteral agents too; they are GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors.
question: A 60-year-old male patient requires percutaneous coronary intervention. He was given an IV infusion of a reversible ADP receptor inhibitor. Which of the following drugs was used?

explanationHtml:
X- Aspirin and Y- Vorapaxar are the drugs administered to the patient.

Aspirin reduces thromboxane A2 production by inhibiting the COX-1 enzyme.

Vorapaxar is a competitive antagonist of PAR-1 and inhibits thrombin-induced platelet aggregation. Vorapaxar is indicated in combination with aspirin and/or clopidogrel to reduce thromboembolic events in patients with MI or peripheral vascular disease.
question: After suffering from a myocardial infarction, a patient was started on two drugs X and Y. The drug X inhibits the COX-1 enzyme and drug Y inhibits thrombin-induced platelet aggregation. Identify the drugs.

explanationHtml:
Alteplase differs from streptokinase as it has more affinity towards plasminogen bound to fibrin than plasminogen in circulation.

Streptokinase activates both free and fibrin-bound plasminogen.

Other options:

Option A: Rapid clearance by the liver and inactivation by plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 make alteplase shorter-acting than streptokinase.

Among the given options, ischaemic stroke in the past 3 months and suspected aortic dissection are absolute contraindications to fibrinolytic therapy.

This is due to an increased risk of adverse outcomes in patients with a history of ischemic stroke in the last 3 months and a risk for a serious bleed in suspected dissections. Fibrinolysis can be done in patients 3 months after their most recent stroke, as the overall risk is considered lower and offers more benefits.

Active peptic ulcer and uncontrolled hypertension are relative contraindications for fibrinolytic therapy. Menstruation is not a contraindication to fibrinolytic therapy.

Note: History of a hemorrhagic stroke at any time is an absolute contraindication for thrombolytic therapy.
question:

Anistreplase is not a recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA).

Anistreplase (anisoylated plasminogen streptokinase activator complex) is a preformed complex of human plasminogen and bacterial streptokinase, used as a thrombolytic agent.
question: Which of the following is not a recombinant tissue-type plasminogen activator?

explanationHtml:
Tenecteplase can be administered as a single bolus dose for patients requiring coronary thrombolysis.

Other options:

Options A and D: Alteplase and anistreplase are administered as intravenous infusion.

question: Which of the following plasminogen activator can be administered as a single bolus dose for a patient who requires coronary thrombolysis?

explanationHtml:
The given scenario is of a patient who has heavy menstrual bleeding. Tranexamic acid is the drug approved for treating heavy menstrual bleeding.

It is a lysine analogue that binds to the active site of plasmin and prevents the interaction of fibrin with plasmin. This prevents the dissolution of clots and decreases bleeding.

Other options:

Option A: Mefenamic acid is an NSAID and indicated in primary dysmenorrhea.

Option C: ε-Aminocaproic acid is also an antifibrinolytic agent like tranexamic acid. However, it is not approved for heavy menstrual bleeding.

Option D: Acetylsalicylic acid is aspirin, an anti-platelet drug.
question: A 35-year-old woman came to the gynecology OPD with a history of heavy menstrual bleeding. She complained of having to change 4-5 pads in a day and an increase in bleeding to more than 7 days since the last few months. Which of the following is the preferred drug that can be given to this patient?

explanationHtml:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of post-thrombolytic hemorrhagic transformation of an ischemic stroke. ε-Aminocaproic acid can be used as an antidote for fibrinolytic therapy.

It is a lysine analog that binds competitively to plasminogen, blocking plasminogen from binding to fibrin and the subsequent conversion to plasmin. This activity subsequently results in the inhibition of fibrinolysis.

It should not be given unless hemorrhage is life-threatening because it inhibits intrinsic fibrinolytic activity and can precipitate DIC. Fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate may also be used to replenish fibrin and clotting factors.

question: A 55-year-old man admitted with ischemic stroke was given IV alteplase. After 8 hours, the ICU staff noticed decreasing mental status and acute hypertension in the patient. A repeat CT revealed the following, Which of the following drugs can be used to manage this patient?

explanationHtml:

It acts as an irreversible ADP (P2 Y12) antagonist and is converted into its active metabolite by CYP3A5 and CYP2B6. Since omeprazole is an inhibitor of CYP2C19, it does not interfere with its activation.

Preconceptional intake of vitamin B9 (folic acid) can lead to decreased incidences of neural tube defects like spina bifida, encephalocele, and anencephaly.

All women of reproductive age should be given 400 µg of folic acid daily. Women who had fetal neural tube defects in the previous pregnancy should be given 4 mg of folic acid daily beginning 1 month before conception to about 12 weeks of pregnancy.
question: A newly married couple planning for pregnancy has come to your clinic for preconception counselling. Which of the following drugs will you prescribe to the patient to decrease the chances of having neural tube defects in the baby?

explanationHtml:
Among the following, chloroquine is the least likely drug to precipitate folic acid deficiency.

The drugs that can result in the deficiency of folic acid include anticonvulsants (phenytoin, primidone), oral contraceptives, and dihydrofolate reductase inhibitors (trimethoprim, sulfasalazine, methotrexate). Megaloblastic anemia can be caused by a deficiency of folic acid or vitamin B12.

A mnemonic for the causes of megaloblastic anemia is: Prime BATSMAN

  • Prime – phenytoin, primidone
  • B – B12 and folate deficiency
  • A – alcohol
  • T – Trimethoprim
  • S – Sulfasalazine

question: A 25-year-old patient has subclinical folate deficiency. Which of the following drugs is least likely to precipitate megaloblastic anaemia in this patient?

explanationHtml:
The absorption of iron is impeded by egg-based foods. They contain a high amount of phosphates (egg yolk) that form complexes with iron and impede absorption.

Heme-based iron, present in meat products, is easily absorbed without the aid of a carrier and is not much affected by other foods. Inorganic iron is affected by several factors.

Factors increasing iron absorption are:

  • Reducing substances such as ascorbic acid and amino acids containing –SH groups - reduce ferric iron to the soluble ferrous form
  • Meat-based foods - enhance heme absorption and increase acid secretion.

Factors decreasing iron absorption are:

  • Phosphates, phytates, and tetracyclines - by forming complexes
  • Alkalies - prevents the reduction of ferric iron to the soluble ferrous form
  • Presence of other food in the stomach - by increasing pH
question: Absorption of iron is impeded by which of the following?

explanationHtml:
In an anemic patient with IBD, parenteral iron is preferred over oral formulations. The parenteral formulation of iron among the given options is ferrous sucrose.

On intravenous administration, it is taken up by reticuloendothelial cells where it dissociates and iron is utilized.

The formulations used for parenteral iron therapy are:

  • Iron dextran
  • Iron - sorbitol - citric acid
  • Ferrous sucrose
  • Ferric carboxy maltose

Ferrous sulfate, ferrous gluconate, and ferrous fumarate are oral iron preparations.
question: When treating an anemic patient with a history of inflammatory bowel disease, which of the following iron formulations will you prefer?

explanationHtml:
Erythropoietin decreases the need for blood transfusions and increases reticulocyte counts.

Therapeutic uses and effects of erythropoietin:

  • The primary indication of erythropoietin is anaemia due to chronic renal failure
  • It causes functional iron deficiency due to the inability to mobilize iron stores rapidly enough to support the increased erythropoiesis (low transferrin saturation)
  • It increases the hematocrit, haemoglobin, and reduces the need for transfusions
  • It aggravates hypertension due to an increase in hematocrit and leads to thrombus formation
  • Reticulocyte count is elevated, due to premature release of immature red blood cells (reticulocytes) from the bone marrow into the bloodstream.
question:

explanationHtml:
Darbepoetin alpha is the recombinant derivative of erythropoietin that is long-acting and approved for anaemia due to chronic renal failure.

Darbepoetin alpha is modified to have a 3-fold longer half-life than recombinant human EPO (e.g., epoetin alfa/beta), allowing less frequent dosing, and better patient compliance.

Other options:

Option A: Oprelvekin is an IL-11 analog that stimulates megakaryocyte maturation.

Option C: Dornase alfa is a recombinant human DNase 1 that is used in cystic fibrosis to reduce the viscosity of mucosal secretions.

question: In a patient with anaemia due to chronic renal failure, which of the following is the long-acting derivative of erythropoietin suitable for treatment?

explanationHtml:
Sargramostim is a recombinant human GM-CSF (Granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor).

Indications for use:

  • Cancer chemotherapy - reduces the duration of neutropenia
  • Peripheral blood stem cell collection - to mobilize CD34 positive progenitor cells

question: Sargramostim is a recombinantly engineered analogue of which of the following?

correctAnswer: C. It should not be administered in sickle cell patients
explanationHtml:
Patients with sickle cell anemia should not receive pegylated filgrastim as it can trigger a sickle cell crisis.

Filgrastim is a recombinant human G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor). The pegylated forms of filgrastim, pegfilgrastim, and lipefilgrastim, are longer-acting forms. It is administered subcutaneously or by slow intravenous infusion only.

Indications of recombinant G-CSF:

  • Severe neutropenia after autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation
  • Severe neutropenia after high dose cancer chemotherapy
  • Severe congenital neutropenias
  • Neutropenia of patients with AIDS receiving zidovudine

Romiplostim, eltrombopag, and lusutrombopag are thrombopoietin receptor agonists. They are indicated in patients with immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) who have failed to respond to conventional treatments.
question: Which of the following is not a thrombopoietin receptor agonist?

explanationHtml:
Oprelvekin is used in the treatment of thrombocytopenia secondary to anti-cancer therapy.

It is a recombinant human interleukin-11. Its predominant hemopoietic activity is the stimulation of megakaryocytopoiesis. Oprelvekin is indicated for the prevention and treatment of severe thrombocytopenia and the reduction of platelet transfusion requirements following myelosuppressive chemotherapy in patients with non-myeloid malignancies.

Other options:

Option A: Filgrastim is a G-CSF that stimulates the growth of neutrophils and is used in cancer patients with neutropenia.
question: Which of the following agents is used in the treatment of patients who develop severe thrombocytopenia following anti-cancer therapy?

explanationHtml:
Plerixafor is the CXCR-4 antagonist indicated for peripheral blood stem cell mobilization before autologous stem cell transplantation.

It is indicated for peripheral blood stem cell mobilization in patients with Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and multiple myeloma having inadequate response to G-CSF. It mobilizes the release and entry of HSCs from the bone marrow into circulation. Peripheral blood stem cell mobilization/collection is followed by autologous transplantation.

Other options:

Option A: Maraviroc is a CCR-5 receptor inhibitor indicated in HIV infections.

Options B and C: Sargramostim (GM-CSF) and filgrastim (G-CSF) are used for peripheral blood stem cell mobilization.
question: A patient requires autologous stem cell transplantation due to multiple myeloma. A CXCR-4 antagonist which mobilizes stem cells to the peripheral blood is administered few weeks before the procedure. Identify the drug.

explanationHtml:
Avatrombopag is a thrombopoietin receptor agonist approved for the treatment of thrombocytopenia with chronic liver disease in patients who are scheduled to undergo a medical or dental procedure.

Thrombopoietin receptor agonist stimulates proliferation and differentiation of megakaryocytes from bone marrow progenitor cells, resulting in increased production of platelets. Lusutrombopag is a drug with similar action and function.

Other options:

Options A & B: Eltrombopag and romiplostim are thrombopoietin receptor agonists indicated in chronic immune thrombocytopenia.

Option C: Oprelvekin is a recombinant IL-11 that is used in the prophylaxis of thrombocytopenia during cancer chemotherapy.
question: A patient having chronic liver disease is set to undergo a tooth extraction. During pre-op evaluation, his platelet count is found to be 60 x 10^9/ L. Which thrombopoietin receptor agonist can you prescribe to treat this?

explanationHtml:
The scenario in the question depicts a case of chronic immune thrombocytopenia which can be treated with a tyrosine kinase inhibitor called fostamatinib.

Fostamatinib has activity against spleen tyrosine kinase (SYK). The major metabolite of fostamatinib, R406, inhibits signal transduction of Fc-activating receptors and B-cell receptors. The fostamatinib metabolite R406 reduces antibody-mediated destruction of platelets.

Other options:

Option A: Romiplostim is a TPO receptor agonist indicated in chronic immune thrombocytopenia.

Option B: Bosutinib is a BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor indicated in CML.

Option D: Oprelvekin is a recombinant IL-11 that is used in the prophylaxis of thrombocytopenia during cancer chemotherapy.
question: A 26-year-old woman presented to the OPD with multiple purpuric lesions. Further workup revealed isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal peripheral smear. Which tyrosine kinase inhibitor is indicated in her treatment?

explanationHtml:
The primary mechanism of action of heparin is by activation of antithrombin.

In patients with atrial fibrillation that has persisted for more than 48 hours, heparin can be used to reduce the risk of thrombus formation and embolization until the warfarin level is therapeutic or cardioversion is performed.

Heparin, low molecular weight heparin (LMWHs), and fondaparinux have no intrinsic anticoagulant activity. They bind to antithrombin and accelerates the rate at which it inhibits various coagulation proteases, especially thrombin (factor IIa) and factor Xa.

LMWH has some action against thrombin. However, fondaparinux has no action against thrombin. Antithrombin inhibits these factors by serving as a “suicide substrate”.
question: A patient with sustained atrial fibrillation was given heparin cover. What is the primary mechanism of action of the drug?

explanationHtml:
Hypokalemia is least likely seen in this patient because heparin-induced hypoaldosteronism causes hyperkalemia.

Heparin inhibits aldosterone synthesis by reducing adrenal angiotensin II receptors. This inturn leads to hyperkalemia and salt wasting. This effect is very potent and dose-dependent, and the effects can be seen as early as 3-4 days.

aPTT is prolonged in heparin therapy and is used to monitor its anticoagulant effect.

The side effects of heparin are (OATH):

  • O - Osteoporosis
  • A - Alopecia (reversible)
  • T - Thrombocytopenia (Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia - HIT)
  • H - Hemorrhage, Hyperkalemia
question: A patient is receiving low dose heparin infusions after hip replacement surgery to prevent thromboembolism. Which of the following abnormalities are least likely to be expected in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Antithrombin-III is mandatory for the action of heparin as an anticoagulant. Reduced antithrombin levels can lead to resistance.

Heparin resistance refers to failure to achieve a therapeutic aPTT with daily doses of heparin of 35,000 units or more.

In true heparin resistance, there is an actual blunting of heparin’s anticoagulant effect. This occurs due to:

  • Low ATIII levels (most common cause)
  • Increased heparin-binding plasma proteins (acute phase reactants)
  • Increased heparin clearance (e.g. due to splenomegaly in liver disease)

Low ATIII levels could be due to decreased synthesis (hereditary, hepatic failure), increased consumption (DIC, MAHA, or in a bypass circuit) or increased loss (nephrotic syndrome).

The dose of heparin has to be increased to achieve therapeutic aPTT. Severe antithrombin deficiency may require antithrombin concentrate as well.

[[figure-1]]
question: For the action of heparin as an anticoagulant, availability of which of the following chemical substances is mandatory?

explanationHtml:
Protamine sulfate is the drug used to treat life-threatening, heparin-induced bleeding.

The drug antagonism between heparin and protamine sulfate is an example of chemical antagonism. Protamine sulfate is a mixture of basic polypeptides that are positively charged. They bind to the highly acidic heparin with a strong negative charge and form protamine-heparin complexes that are cleared.

It is a mixture of basic polypeptides isolated from salmon sperm. It binds to acidic heparin with high affinity and neutralizes anticoagulant activity. The resultant protamine-heparin complexes are cleared. Protamine binds only to long heparin molecules (UFH). Therefore, protamine only partially reverses the activity of LMWH and has no effect on fondaparinux.

It is most commonly used to neutralize heparin-induced anticoagulation after separation from cardiopulmonary bypass. It is also utilized in the setting of dialysis, invasive vascular procedures, and acute ischemic strokes.

Note: Protamine sulfate has anticoagulant activity at higher doses and hence, only small amounts of protamine (1mg/100 units of heparin) are used for heparin-induced bleeding.
question: A patient scheduled for a CABG procedure receives preoperative heparin for anticoagulation. During the surgery, the patient starts bleeding massively and there is a drop in BP. Which of the following would you use to manage this patient?

explanationHtml:
Low-molecular-weight heparin(LMWH) has predominant activity against factor Xa.

LMWH has an anti-factor activity against both Xa and IIa with a greater effect on Xa.
question: Predominant activity of low-molecular-weight heparin is seen against which clotting factor?

explanationHtml:
LMWH is given by the subcutaneous route.

Heparin, low molecular weight heparin (LMWH), and fondaparinux are not absorbed through GI mucosa and must be given parenterally. LMWH and fondaparinux are given subcutaneously.

Heparin can be given through intravenous infusion and subcutaneous routes.
question: LMWH is given by which route?

correctAnswer: A. Is absorbed more uniformly when given subcutaneously
explanationHtml:
Enoxaparin (LMWH) has a very high bioavailability and is absorbed more uniformly when compared to unfractionated heparin. Hence, it does not require frequent monitoring.

LMWH can also lead to heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) and hence, it cannot be given in patients with HIT.

LMWH preparations:

  • Enoxaparin
  • Dalteparin
  • Tinzaparin.

options.text: Is absorbed more uniformly when given subcutaneously
Can be given to patients with heparin induced thrombocytopenia
Predisposes to a higher risk of osteopenia

question: As compared to unfractionated heparin, which of the following is true about enoxaparin?

explanationHtml:
The anticoagulant of choice for the management of cancer-associated thromboembolism is low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH).

It is the preferred agent because of its higher bioavailability, lack of need for anticoagulant monitoring, and a long t1/2.

Venous thromboembolism (including deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and splanchnic vein thrombosis) is a frequent complication of cancer and is the second-leading cause of death in cancer patients receiving chemotherapy.

Based on the results from the Comparison of Low-molecular-weight heparin vs. Oral anticoagulants for long-term anticoagulation in cancer patients with venous Thromboembolism (CLOT) Trial, all recent guidelines now advise LMWH for cancer-associated thromboembolism. However, unfractionated heparin (UFH) can be used in patients with renal failure, and fondaparinux can be considered in patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT).
question: Which is the anticoagulant of choice for the management of cancer-associated thromboembolism?

explanationHtml:
Unfractionated heparin is the anticoagulant of choice for patients requiring cardiopulmonary bypass.

Cardiopulmonary bypass circuits activate factor XII which can lead to clotting in the oxygenator. This process is called catheter-induced thrombosis.

Unfractionated heparin is better than LMWH or fondaparinux for blocking it. Also, reversal of anticoagulation using protamine sulfate is easier for UFH compared to the other heparins.

Note: In patients with a history of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, bivalirudin has recently gained recognition for use in cardiopulmonary bypass.
question: A 65-year-old patient has been scheduled for cardiopulmonary bypass surgery. Which is the anticoagulant of choice for this patient?

explanationHtml:
The most common presentation of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is venous thrombosis.

HIT is an immune complication of heparin therapy caused by IgG antibodies against the heparin-platelet factor 4 complex. This results in the activation of platelets to propagate a hypercoagulable state culminating in life-threatening thrombosis.

It is characterized by thrombocytopenia (Platelet count <1,00,000/μL or reduced by over 50% from pre-treatment value) and clinically presents as venous thrombosis (in the form of DVT or pulmonary embolism)

It occurs around 5-10 days after starting heparin. It is more common with UFH when compared to LMWH. It is also more common in women surgical patients. Arterial thrombosis (resulting in MI or stroke), as well as bilateral adrenal hemorrhage, can rarely occur.

question: Lab reports of a 45-year-old female patient, who was recently started on heparin, showed rapidly falling platelet counts. She was suspected to have heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. What is the most common presentation seen in this condition?

correctAnswer: D. Heparin should be replaced with warfarin
explanationHtml:
The patient in the above scenario has heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT). Direct thrombin inhibitors, such as argatroban is the anticoagulant of choice in HIT.

Management of HIT:

  • Stop heparin/LMWH
  • Give an alternative anticoagulant, such as lepirudin, argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux or rivaroxaban
  • Do not give platelet transfusions (it only worsens the consumptive coagulopathy)
  • Do not give warfarin until the platelet count returns to its baseline level. If warfarin was administered, give vitamin K to restore the INR to normal.

Increased thrombin generation associated with HIT can cause consumption of protein C. Warfarin administration can further decrease protein C levels and cause skin necrosis. Therefore warfarin is avoided in HIT.

options.text: Alternative anticoagulant such as argatroban should be administered
Low molecular weight heparins should be avoided
Heparin should be replaced with warfarin

question: A 64-year-old man was started on heparin postoperatively for thromboprophylaxis. After a week he developed sudden difficulty in breathing. His platelet count was found to be 70,000/microliter. Which of the following is incorrect regarding the management of this patient?

explanationHtml:
Since no effect was noted with protamine sulfate, the likely anticoagulant in use must be fondaparinux. This is because protamine sulfate fails to bind the drug.

Fondaparinux is an antithrombin activator. It is a synthetic analog of the pentasaccharide unit of heparin that binds and activates antithrombin. Activation of antithrombin causes the inactivation of factor Xa. So it is also described as an indirect factor Xa inhibitor.

It is not a direct factor Xa inhibitor. Direct factor Xa inhibitors include rivaroxaban, apixaban, and edoxaban

Protamine sulfate binds tightly to heparin and neutralizes its anticoagulant effect. It partially reverses the anticoagulant activity of LMWH also. But it has no effect on fondaparinux.

There is no known specific antidote approved for use in fondaparinux overdose. Fondaparinux-associated bleeding complications are managed by treatment discontinuation and search for the primary cause. Surgical hemostasis, blood replacements, fresh plasma transfusion, plasmapheresis should be considered.
question: A patient on anticoagulant therapy presented to the casualty with an uncontrolled bleeding episode and was given IV protamine sulfate. However, the patient did not respond to the treatment. Which of the following anticoagulant agents was most likely being used by the patient?

explanationHtml:
Among the given options, the direct thrombin inhibitor is bivalirudin.

Bivalirudin is a parenteral direct thrombin inhibitor (DTI) frequently used for anticoagulation in invasive cardiology, particularly percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Unlike other DTIs, it undergoes predominant non-organ elimination (proteolysis) and has the shortest half-life (approximately 25 min).

It can be used in patients with, or at risk for, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

Other options:

Options A and D: Enoxaparin and dalteparin are low-molecular-weight-heparin (LMWH) preparations.

Option C: Fondaparinux is a synthetic analog of the pentasaccharide unit of heparin.

Heparins and their analogs produce anticoagulant effects indirectly by activating antithrombin-III.
question: A clinical trial is done to compare the safety profile of a certain direct thrombin inhibitor (drug X) with that of heparin in patients undergoing coronary angioplasty. Identify drug X.

explanationHtml:
The oral thrombin inhibitor which can be used for the prevention of stroke in patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation is dabigatran. However, it is contraindicated in patients with mechanical heart valves.

Dabigatran is a reversible, competitive inhibitor of free and clot-bound thrombin (Factor IIa). It does not require monitoring (INR) and does not have any dietary restrictions. In case of severe bleeding, idarucizumab can be used as an antidote.

Other options:

Option B: Ximelagatran is also an oral thrombin inhibitor, but it has been discontinued due to the risk of hepatotoxicity.

Option C: Lepirudin is a parenteral direct thrombin inhibitor used mainly in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

Option D: Saxagliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor used in the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus.
question: The oral thrombin inhibitor which can be used for prevention of stroke in patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation is?

explanationHtml:
The parenteral direct thrombin inhibitor is argatroban.

Argatroban binds reversibly to thrombin and inhibits it. It is metabolized in the liver and excreted in bile, so it can be safely used in patients with renal impairment.

It can be used for prophylaxis and treatment of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT).

Other parenteral direct thrombin inhibitors are their indications:

  • Lepirudin - was indicated in HIT but is discontinued now
  • Desirudin - indicated for thromboprophylaxis in hip replacement surgery
  • Bivalirudin - used in procedures like coronary angioplasty or cardiopulmonary bypass surgery and HIT.
question: Which of the following is a parenteral direct thrombin inhibitor?

explanationHtml:
Rivaroxaban is an oral direct factor Xa inhibitor. They represent a new class of oral anticoagulant drugs that do not require monitoring.

This group of drugs inhibits the factor Xa in the final common pathway of clotting [conversion of Prothrombin (Factor II) to thrombin (Factor IIa)]. They are given as fixed doses and have a rapid onset of action.

Oral direct factor Xa inhibitors are indicated in:

  • Prevention of embolic stroke in patients with atrial fibrillation (without valvular heart disease)
  • Venous thromboembolic disease (VTE)
  • Postoperative thromboprophylaxis in patients undergoing hip and knee arthroplasty
question: Which of the following is an oral factor Xa inhibitor?

explanationHtml:
Idarucizumab is a reversal agent for dabigatran.

Idarucizumab is a humanized mouse monoclonal antibody fragment. It binds irreversibly to dabigatran and forms a complex that is cleared by the kidneys.
question: A patient with a history of regular oral anticoagulant therapy suffers a traumatic injury. He receives idarucizumab before damage control surgery to reverse the anticoagulant effect. Identify the oral anticoagulant that was being used by the patient.

explanationHtml:
Ciraparantag shows a reversal in the action of all direct anticoagulants (dabigatran and other oral factor Xa inhibitors) and also heparin and LMWH. It is a synthetic cationic molecule which is still under trial.

Other options:

Option A: Protamine sulfate reverses the action of heparin and LMWH.

Option B: Idarucizumab is a specific antidote for dabigatran overdose.

Option C: Andexanet alfa is a decoy for oral factor Xa inhibitors.
question: Which of the following drugs is under clinical trials and shows a reversal in the action of all direct anticoagulants?

explanationHtml:
Coagulation profile monitoring is needed for lepirudin.

Lepirudin is a direct, irreversible thrombin inhibitor, and its most adverse reaction is bleeding. The risk of bleeding can be reduced by implementing an appropriate monitoring and dose adjustment strategy. Additionally, lepirudin does not have an antidote. Thus, coagulation profile monitoring is required for lepirudin.

Enoxaparin, fondaparinux, and dabigatran do not bind to the endothelium or many plasma proteins. The response to these drugs at the usual doses is consistent from patient to patient, so they're given at a fixed dose normally. Hence, monitoring is not required.
question: Coagulation profile monitoring is needed in therapy with which of the following drugs?

explanationHtml:
Heparin is the anticoagulant that can be safely used in pregnancy in the first trimester.

Heparin, LMWH, and fondaparinux do not cross the blood-brain barrier or placenta, and hence they are the anticoagulants preferred in pregnancy.

Warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists are contraindicated during pregnancy due to the risk of teratogenicity. This is mainly during the first trimester, where warfarin causes stippled epiphyses and can lead to malformations. Warfarin can be used in the second and third trimesters if it is required, but is generally avoided due to the teratogenicity warning.
question: Which of the following anticoagulants can be safely used in a pregnant patient in the first trimester?

explanationHtml:
Warfarin directly inhibits the enzyme Vitamin K epoxide reductase.

It inhibits the conversion of vitamin K epoxide to its reduced form - vitamin K hydroquinone, which is a cofactor for the enzyme gamma-glutamyl carboxylase. This enzyme catalyzes the γ-carboxylation process of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors.

[[figure-1]]

Warfarin is primarily metabolized by CYP2C9. Genetic polymorphisms of CYP2C9 and drugs inhibiting or inducing CYP2C9 can result in variable responses to warfarin administration.
question: A patient is on DVT prophylaxis with warfarin. It has an inhibitory action on which of the following enzymes?

explanationHtml:
Factor VII is a vitamin K dependant clotting factor.

The vitamin K dependent factors:

  • Clotting factors: Factors II, VII, IX, X

question: Which of the following is vitamin K dependent clotting factor?

question: A patient suffering from non-valvular atrial fibrillation is prescribed warfarin tablets. Which of the following clotting factors would you expect to decline the earliest in this patient after drug administration?

question: In a patient receiving warfarin tablets, which enzyme primarily metabolizes the drug?

explanationHtml:
Carbamazepine does not increase the risk of bleeding in patients undergoing warfarin therapy.

Warfarin is mainly metabolized by the CYP2C9 enzyme. Drugs that inhibit the CYP2C9 enzyme reduce the metabolism of warfarin and thus, enhance the anticoagulant effect of warfarin and increase the risk of bleeding.

Drugs causing CYP2C9 inhibition:

  • Amiodarone
  • Azole antifungals
  • Cimetidine
  • Clopidogrel
  • Cotrimoxazole
  • Disulfiram
  • Isoniazid
  • Metronidazole

Note: CYP2C9 indicates that the enzyme is cytochrome P450 family 2 subfamily C member 9. It is thus a part of the CYP450 family, which encompasses a broader group of enzymes involved in drug metabolism.
question: Which of the following drugs does not increase the risk of bleeding in patients undergoing warfarin therapy?

explanationHtml:
Decreased effect of warfarin is seen in patients with nephrotic syndrome.

Warfarin is highly bound to plasma protein, and in nephrotic syndrome, there is proteinuria. Normally, drugs that are bound to plasma proteins have a longer half-life as there is a reservoir of the drug in the blood bound to the protein. This drug is slowly released from the plasma proteins, thus leading to a longer effect of the drug. Drugs that are bound to plasma proteins are lost in the urine. Thus, warfarin is lost in urine in nephrotic syndrome, resulting in a decreased effect.

Other options:

Option C: Warfarin is mainly metabolized by the CYP2C9 enzyme. In patients being treated with metronidazole (a CYP2C9 inhibitor), the metabolism of warfarin is decreased. Hence, the effect of warfarin is increased.

Options B and D: Hepatic impairment, congestive heart failure, and hyperthyroidism lead to low concentrations of clotting factors, and the effect of warfarin is enhanced in these conditions.
question: While prescribing warfarin, a decreased effect of the drug is expected in patients with which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
Warfarin is a vitamin K epoxide reductase inhibitor prescribed for splanchnic vein thrombosis in this patient. Warfarin therapy is usually monitored by measuring prothrombin time.

Prothrombin time is sensitive to the reduction in levels of prothrombin, factor VII, and factor X. The test is performed by adding thromboplastin, which is a reagent containing tissue factor, phospholipid, and calcium to citrated plasma and determining the time to clot formation.

Due to the variable sensitivity of thromboplastin, the International normalized ratio (INR) was developed to standardize the reporting of prothrombin time. In INR, the patient’s prothrombin time is divided by mean normal prothrombin time and this ratio is multiplied by the International Sensitivity Index (ISI) of the particular thromboplastin reagent.

Warfarin therapy should be monitored with INR every 3–4 weeks. The target INR is 2.0–3.0. In patients with mechanical heart valves, the target INR is 2.5–3.5.
question: A patient with splanchnic vein thrombosis has been started on a vitamin K epoxide reductase inhibitor. Which of the following can be used to monitor the treatment in this patient?

explanationHtml:
This patient has ecchymoses after initiation of treatment with warfarin. The image given shows the characteristic necrotic patches of warfarin-induced skin necrosis, seen due to a congenital or acquired deficiency in either protein C or protein S.

Warfarin therapy in such patients leads to a rapid fall in protein C or protein S, which are vitamin K-dependent anticoagulants. Protein C deficiency is more common than protein S deficiency. This occurs before warfarin can exert an antithrombotic effect.

Warfarin should be discontinued, and vitamin K (the antidote for warfarin) should be administered in these patients, and treatment should be initiated with other anticoagulants such as heparin or LMWH.
question: A 50-year-old patient admitted with atrial fibrillation was started on bisoprolol and warfarin. After 4 days of admission, she started experiencing painful ecchymoses on her right lower limb. It progressed to the condition shown in the image over the next few days. Deficiency in which of the following can lead to this condition?

explanationHtml:
This patient with a raised INR in the background of warfarin therapy, with clinical features of bleeding such as alveolar hemorrhages, has developed warfarin toxicity. Immediate or urgent reversal of warfarin-induced bleeding is best achieved by the administration of prothrombin complex concentrates (PCC).

These are highly purified concentrates prepared from pooled plasma and contain factors II, IX, and X. Factor VII may be included or produced separately. PCCs are preferred over other preparations due to the smaller quantity of infusion required and higher effectiveness in reversing the bleeding manifestations.

Other options:

Option D: Vitamin K1 is the specific antidote for warfarin-induced bleeding, but it takes 6-24 hours for the clotting factors to be resynthesized and released in blood after Vitamin K administration and hence its action is delayed for several hours.

Option A: Cryoprecipitate mainly contains factor VIII and fibrinogen and therefore is not suitable for warfarin-induced bleeding, as warfarin inhibits factors II, VII, IX, and X.

Option B: Fresh frozen plasma can also be used, but prothrombin complex concentrate normalizes the INR more rapidly.
question: A 27-year-old male patient on anticoagulant therapy for his DVT started coughing up blood. He has a history of irregular warfarin intake. Workup revealed elevated INR and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage. Which of the following agents would be the best choice for immediate reversal of bleeding?

Macrocephaly is not a fetal abnormality caused by warfarin administered during pregnancy.

Warfarin can cross the placenta, but doesn't enter breast milk; therefore, it can be given to lactating mothers.

Effects of warfarin during pregnancy:

  • Stippled epiphysis
  • Nasal hypoplasia

The risk of embryopathy is highest with exposure in the first trimester of pregnancy. Exposure in the second and third trimesters can lead to abnormalities in the central nervous system

question: In patients with indications for warfarin usage, what is the recommended range of INR necessary for safe administration of the drug?

Apixaban, a novel oral anticoagulant (NOAC), is a factor Xa inhibitor that is used in the treatment of VTE (venous thromboembolism)/DVT and in its prophylaxis after major orthopedic surgeries.

Direct factor Xa inhibitors include rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban, and betrixaban.

Note: The FDA recently approved the drug apixaban for a new indication. The drug is now used to reduce the risk of stroke and systemic embolism in patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation.
question: Apixaban belongs to which of the following class of drugs?

correctAnswer: C. In combination with an inhaled corticosteroid
explanationHtml:
LABA is used in combination with inhalational corticosteroids (ICS), preferably in the form of a combination inhaler.

LABA is never taken alone as it does not treat the underlying chronic inflammation of asthma. Corticosteroids will decrease the underlying inflammation and halt the progression of the disease.

Short-acting β-2 agonists (SABA) can be given as an add-on therapy to the LABA-ICS combination (as-needed therapy).

Beta 2 agonists are classified based on their duration of action into:

  • Short-acting β2 agonists (SABA): Salbutamol, terbutaline, pirbuterol
  • Long-acting β2 agonists (LABA): Formoterol, salmeterol
  • Very long-acting β2 agonists (V-LABA): Indacaterol, olodaterol, vilanterol

question:
What is the current GINA recommendation for the prescription of long-acting β-2 agonists in patients suffering from bronchial asthma?

GINA: Global Initiative for Asthma

explanationHtml:
Nebulized short-acting beta-2 agonists (SABAs) are the most appropriate therapy in acute severe asthma among the given options.

SABA has a rapid onset, targeting the bronchial smooth muscles and causing bronchodilation. The nebulized route is preferred over the intravenous route as it is easier and safer with equivalent efficacy. (Option D)

Intravenous aminophylline is less effective than SABA and is reserved for those who are resistant or intolerant to beta-2 agonists with acute severe asthma. (Option A)

Inhalational anticholinergics can be used as an adjunct in the management of acute asthma for additional bronchodilation, but not as a single therapy. (Option B)
question: Which among the following is the most appropriate therapy for bronchodilation in acute severe asthma?

explanationHtml:
Hypoglycemia is not a side effect of salbutamol. It causes hyperglycemia by β2 receptor-mediated glycogenolysis and glucagon release.

The side effects of salbutamol are due to the stimulation of extrapulmonary β2 receptors. They are more common after oral or intravenous administration. The side effects seen are:

  • Musculoskeletal tremors: Stimulation of β2 receptors in skeletal muscles. (Option C)
  • Tachycardia: Reflex sympathetic stimulation due to vasodilator action on β2 receptors and direct effect on cardiac β1 receptors (β2 selectivity is lost at high concentrations). (Option D)
  • Hypokalemia: Effect on the Na+/K+-ATPase on the cell membranes, causing inward shift of potassium into the cells, potentially leading to low serum potassium levels; and because of this effect, salbutamol is also used in the management of acute hyperkalemia. (Option B)
  • Restlessness
  • Hypoxemia
  • Increase in free fatty acid, insulin, glucose, pyruvate, and lactate
  • Tolerance: Desensitisation on long-term use
question: Which of the following is not a side effect of salbutamol?

This patient has persistent asthma for which the preferred therapy is LABA with ICS available as a combination inhaler.

ICS should be started in any patient who needs to use a short-acting beta-2 agonist inhaler for symptomatic control more than twice a week (persistent asthma).
question: An asthmatic patient complains of wheezing and shortness of breath most days of the week. Which of the following therapies is preferred in him?

correctAnswer: C. Increases the incidence of oropharyngeal candidiasis
explanationHtml:
The given image is of a spacer device. It decreases the incidence of oropharyngeal candidiasis and other propellant-mediated oropharyngeal adverse effects like dysphonia that occur with the use of a pMDI.

Spacers reduce the velocity and size of particles entering the upper airways. This reduces the amount of drug that impinges on the oropharynx and increases the proportion of drug inhaled into lower airways. The systemic absorption is unchanged by the use of a spacer.

Spacer devices are useful in delivering inhaled drugs to children who are not able to use a pMDI alone but can also be used by adults for better drug delivery. The image below shows the use of a spacer device with a face mask which is preferred in children younger than 3 years of age.

[[figure-1]]

The various devices used for the delivery of inhalational drugs are:

  • Pressurized metered-dose inhalers - Drugs are propelled from a canister in the pMDI with the aid of a propellant. These devices are convenient, portable, and typically deliver 50–200 doses of a drug

[[figure-2]]

  • Dry powder inhalers - these devices scatter the drug into a fine powder that is dispersed by air turbulence on inhalation. DPIs have been developed to deliver drugs such as insulin, but the dosing is inconsistent. Children <7 years find it difficult to use a DPI.

[[figure-3]]

  • Nebulizers: Two types of nebulizer are available -
    • Jet nebulizers that are driven by a stream of gas (air or oxygen)
    • Ultrasonic nebulizers that use a rapidly vibrating piezoelectric crystal and thus do not require a source of compressed gas.

The nebulizers deliver much higher drug doses as compared pMDIs. These are useful in:

  • Treating acute exacerbations of asthma and COPD
  • Extreme airway obstruction (severe COPD)
  • Delivering inhaled drugs to infants and small children who cannot use the other inhalation devices
  • Administering drugs such as antibiotics in relatively high doses

[[figure-4]]

question: A 5-year-old child requires bronchodilator therapy. You attach the device shown below to the pressurized metered-dose inhaler for ease of use. Which of the following is false about this device?

explanationHtml:
Theophylline has an antagonistic action on adenosine receptors.

Theophylline is a methylxanthine. It acts as a non-selective PDE inhibitor. Its other actions include:

  • Increased IL-10 release
  • Decrease in gene transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines
  • Promotes apoptosis of granulocytes
  • Histone deacetylase activation. The recruitment of histone deacetylase-2 by glucocorticoid receptors switches off inflammatory genes. Through this mechanism, theophylline enhances the anti-inflammatory effects of corticosteroids.

Theophylline can be used as a bronchodilator in an asthmatic patient on ICS as an add-on drug. LABAs are more effective but theophylline is a cheaper option.
question: An asthmatic patient has been taking theophylline tablets for symptomatic relief. On which of the following receptors does this drug have an antagonistic action?

correctAnswer: A. Increase in dose is required in cardiopulmonary disease
explanationHtml:
A decrease in the dose of theophylline is required in cardiopulmonary disease. This is because reduced clearance of theophylline is seen in liver disease, pneumonia, and heart failure.

Theophylline is a methylxanthine drug used in the management of asthma as an add-on drug and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. It is a non-selective phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor that decreases the breakdown of cAMP levels in smooth muscles, resulting in bronchodilation (Option B & D). Other mechanisms for anti-inflammation include antagonistic action on adenosine receptors, increased IL-10 and enhancement of histone deacetylation.

Theophylline is mainly metabolised by the CYP1A2 enzyme. Various drug interactions of theophylline include:

  • Increased clearance (CYP1A2 enzyme induction) by smoking, phenytoin, rifampicin, and phenobarbitone. (Option C)
  • Decreased clearance (CYP1A2 enzyme inhibition) by erythromycin, cimetidine, ciprofloxacin, oral contraceptives, and allopurinol.

Important side effects of this drug due to PDE4 antagonism are nausea, vomiting, and gastric discomfort, and those due to adenosine A1 receptor antagonism are diuresis, cardiac arrhythmias, and seizures.

Decreases the breakdown of cAMP in smooth muscles
Increase in dose is required in smokers

question: Which of the following statements about theophylline is not correct?

explanationHtml:
Theophylline is indicated in the treatment of apnea of prematurity.

In apnea of prematurity, methylxanthines such as theophylline and caffeine increase the central respiratory drive by lowering the threshold of response to hypercapnia. They also enhance the contractility of the diaphragm and prevent diaphragmatic fatigue.

Other options:

Options A & B: The adenosine receptor antagonism property of theophylline precipitates cardiac arrhythmias and epileptic seizures.

Option C: Theophylline is no longer recommended as a treatment for acute severe asthma by the latest GINA guidelines because of its poor efficacy and safety profile.
question: Which of the following is an indication for theophylline?

explanationHtml:
Zafirlukast and montelukast are leukotriene receptor antagonists. They are competitive antagonists of the cysLT1 receptors. These drugs act by:

  • Decreasing bronchoconstriction
  • Reducing airway mucus secretion
  • Decreasing vascular permeability and
  • Reducing eosinophil chemotaxis

Other options:

Option A: Dupilumab is an interleukin-4 receptor antagonist used in severe asthma.

Option B: Roflumilast is a PDE-4 selective inhibitor used in the treatment of COPD.

Option D: Zileuton is a 5-lipoxygenase inhibitor that can be used in the treatment of asthma.
question: A patient with severe, persistent asthma continues to have symptoms despite being on high-dose ICS-LABA therapy. Which of the following is a leukotriene receptor antagonist, appropriate as an add-on therapy for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Zileuton, montelukast, and zafirlukast are all associated with rare instances of hepatic dysfunction. Liver function tests should be monitored during the course of their therapy.

Zileuton can cause hepatoxicity due to its direct toxic effect, rather than a consequence of 5-lipoxygenase inhibition. An increase in serum aminotransferases has been noted during the treatment, therefore, serial monitoring of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) is recommended during the treatment. Additionally, montelukast and zafirlukast have also been associated rarely with hepatobiliary dysfunction.

Therapy with selective β-2 agonists (salbutamol, salmeterol) does not require serial monitoring of LFTs.
question:
